metadata.title: Orthopaedic Question Bank (Orthopedic Surgery & Traumatology)
metadata.description: Multiple-choice questions organized by topics and chapters.

questions.question: A patient presents with acute, rapidly progressing unilateral swelling, intense erythema, and severe pain in the right foot and lower leg as shown in the clinical photograph. The contralateral limb is completely normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Acute, unilateral, rapidly expanding severe extremity edema and erythema in the absence of generalized fluid retention points directly toward a localized envenomation (snake bite) or aggressive localized soft tissue inflammation/infection. Snake venoms contain metalloproteinases, phospholipase A2, and hyaluronidases that induce massive local vascular permeability, tissue necrosis, and severe pain.

High-yield: Unilateral acute lower extremity edema is caused by local processes: deep vein thrombosis (DVT), cellulitis, localized envenomation (snake/spider bite), trauma, or acute compartment syndrome. Bilateral edema reflects systemic disease (cardiac, renal, hepatic).

Exam trap: Never confuse unilateral acute toxic or infectious edema with systemic fluid overload. Systemic causes never present with acute unilateral erythema and severe localized pain.

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Clinical photo showing marked asymmetrical swelling and erythema of the entire right foot and ankle compared to the normal left foot, with clear demarcation and acute localized inflammatory edema.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Acute, unilateral, rapidly expanding severe extremity edema and erythema in the absence of generalized fluid retention points directly toward a localized envenomation (snake bite) or aggressive localized soft tissue inflammation/infection. Snake venoms contain metalloproteinases, phospholipase A2, and hyaluronidases that induce massive local vascular permeability, tissue necrosis, and severe pain.
optionExplanations.B: Congestive heart failure, nephrotic syndrome/renal failure, and cirrhosis/hepatic failure produce dependent, bilateral symmetrical pitting edema due to increased hydrostatic capillary pressure or hypoalbuminemia.
optionExplanations.C: Congestive heart failure, nephrotic syndrome/renal failure, and cirrhosis/hepatic failure produce dependent, bilateral symmetrical pitting edema due to increased hydrostatic capillary pressure or hypoalbuminemia.
optionExplanations.D: Congestive heart failure, nephrotic syndrome/renal failure, and cirrhosis/hepatic failure produce dependent, bilateral symmetrical pitting edema due to increased hydrostatic capillary pressure or hypoalbuminemia.
optionExplanations.E: Pretibial myxedema (Graves disease) or generalized myxedematous skin changes in severe hypothyroidism present with bilateral, non-pitting cutaneous mucinosis rather than acute, unilateral, inflammatory swelling.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify snake bite as a cause of acute unilateral limb swelling and distinguish local toxic/vascular pathology from bilateral systemic causes of edema.

questions.question: A patient presents with buttock pain that progressively radiates to the groin. There is no history of preceding trauma. Pelvic radiography reveals sclerosis, joint space irregular widening, and subchondral erosions bilaterally along the sacroiliac and hip joints (indicated by arrows). What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Radiographic evidence of bilateral sacroiliitis accompanied by peripheral hip joint involvement in an atraumatic presentation is characteristic of seronegative spondyloarthropathies, notably Psoriatic Arthritis (or Ankylosing Spondylitis). In past institutional examination keys, post-septic degenerative sequelae (affecting the sacroiliac/hip complex) has also been credited due to joint destruction patterns.

High-yield: Sacroiliitis is the hallmark of seronegative spondyloarthropathies (PAIR: Psoriatic arthritis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD-associated arthritis, Reactive arthritis). Bilateral symmetrical sacroiliitis is most typical of AS and IBD; psoriatic and reactive can be asymmetrical.

Exam trap: Buttock pain originating from the sacroiliac joint is frequently referred to the groin and posterior thigh, often misdiagnosed as primary hip or lumbar disc pathology.

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Pelvis AP radiograph showing bilateral sacroiliac joint blurring, erosions, and sclerosis (red arrows) with bilateral hip articular involvement (yellow arrows).

[Review note] Source key accepts A or C (post-septic degenerative arthritis credited in past institutional keys). A (psoriatic arthritis/spondyloarthropathy) is kept as the primary answer.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Radiographic evidence of bilateral sacroiliitis accompanied by peripheral hip joint involvement in an atraumatic presentation is characteristic of seronegative spondyloarthropathies, notably Psoriatic Arthritis (or Ankylosing Spondylitis). In past institutional examination keys, post-septic degenerative sequelae (affecting the sacroiliac/hip complex) has also been credited due to joint destruction patterns.
optionExplanations.B: Post-traumatic arthritis requires a verified history of major pelvic ring disruption or acetabular/femoral fractures.
optionExplanations.C: Also accepted by the source key. Radiographic evidence of bilateral sacroiliitis accompanied by peripheral hip joint involvement in an atraumatic presentation is characteristic of seronegative spondyloarthropathies, notably Psoriatic Arthritis (or Ankylosing Spondylitis). In past institutional examination keys, post-septic degenerative sequelae (affecting the sacroiliac/hip complex) has also been credited due to joint destruction patterns.
optionExplanations.D: Gout predominantly affects peripheral acral joints (first MTP) and rarely produces isolated bilateral sacroiliitis.
optionExplanations.E: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease causes unilateral femoral head osteonecrosis in young children (ages 4-8) and does not cause sacroiliitis.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize radiographic sacroiliitis and its association with seronegative spondyloarthropathies like psoriatic arthritis.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes crepitation in orthopedic clinical examination?
questions.explanation:
Crepitation (crepitus) is a palpable or audible crunching, grinding, or crackling sensation produced by the friction between articular surfaces or tendons. In the knee, patellofemoral crepitus is classic in patellofemoral maltracking, chondromalacia patellae, and patellofemoral osteoarthritis as the patella glides abnormally over the trochlear groove.

High-yield: Patellofemoral syndrome is characterized by anterior knee pain exacerbated by stairs, squatting, and prolonged sitting ('theater sign'), frequently accompanied by retropatellar crepitus.

Exam trap: Do not assume crepitus is always pathological or painful; benign physiological crepitus is common without radiographic chondropathy.

optionExplanations.A: Crepitation occurs in any diarthrodial joint (e.g., shoulder, hip, thumb CMC, TMJ) and tendon sheaths.
optionExplanations.B: Crepitation is primarily a tactile sensation (palpable grinding) and secondarily an acoustic phenomenon originating from cartilage wear, bone rubbing, or tenosynovium.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Crepitation (crepitus) is a palpable or audible crunching, grinding, or crackling sensation produced by the friction between articular surfaces or tendons. In the knee, patellofemoral crepitus is classic in patellofemoral maltracking, chondromalacia patellae, and patellofemoral osteoarthritis as the patella glides abnormally over the trochlear groove.
optionExplanations.D: Fine physiological crepitus can be completely painless and asymptomatic in healthy individuals.

questions.educationalObjective: Understand the clinical significance of patellofemoral crepitus in extensor mechanism maltracking.

questions.question: During a physical examination, when the patient stands on the right lower extremity, the unsupported left hemipelvis drops below horizontal as shown in the diagram. Which nerve or muscle injury is directly responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation:
A positive Trendelenburg sign occurs when the pelvis sags on the contralateral unsupported side during single-leg stance. This demonstrates weakness of the hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) of the STANCE leg, which are innervated by the ipsilateral superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1). Standing on the right leg causing left pelvic drop proves a right superior gluteal nerve or right gluteus medius lesion.

High-yield: Trendelenburg Rule: Pelvis drops on the CONTRALATERAL (good/unsupported) side due to weakness on the IPSILATERAL (stance/affected) side (Right stance leg weakness = Left pelvic drop).

Exam trap: Board examiners frequently reverse the sides. Remember: The lesion is on the SIDE OF THE FOOT ON THE GROUND.

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Diagram demonstrating Trendelenburg's sign: stance on right leg leads to downward pelvic tilt on the opposite (left) side, indicating right hip abductor insufficiency.

optionExplanations.A: Gluteus maximus is innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve and functions as the primary hip extensor, not abductor.
optionExplanations.B: Gluteus maximus is innervated by the inferior gluteal nerve and functions as the primary hip extensor, not abductor.
optionExplanations.C: Superior/inferior gluteal arteries supply blood; vascular insufficiency does not directly cause isolated abductor palsy without tissue necrosis.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A positive Trendelenburg sign occurs when the pelvis sags on the contralateral unsupported side during single-leg stance. This demonstrates weakness of the hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) of the STANCE leg, which are innervated by the ipsilateral superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1). Standing on the right leg causing left pelvic drop proves a right superior gluteal nerve or right gluteus medius lesion.
optionExplanations.E: A left superior gluteal nerve injury would cause pelvic sag when standing on the LEFT leg.

questions.educationalObjective: Accurately localize a superior gluteal nerve lesion based on the side of the stance limb during a positive Trendelenburg test.

questions.question: Which of the following represents an ideal, properly structured chief complaint in an orthopedic clinical history?

options.A: Falling down from height caused left thigh pain one hour ago
options.B: Severe pounding pain in the right forearm of 2 days duration
options.D: Left index finger swelling of 3 days duration

questions.explanation:
An ideal chief complaint consists of the patient's primary symptom or physical complaint, exact anatomical location, and specific duration, recorded concisely without diagnostic terminology or narrative history of present illness. 'Left index finger swelling of 3 days duration' perfectly fulfills this standard.

High-yield: Chief Complaint formula: [Primary Symptom] + [Precise Anatomical Site] + [Duration]. Example: 'Right knee pain of 2 weeks duration'.

Exam trap: Do not write diagnostic labels (e.g., 'Gout of first MTP') as the chief complaint; patients present with symptoms, not pre-established diagnoses.

optionExplanations.A: Incorporates narrative mechanism of injury ('falling down from height caused...'), which belongs in the History of Present Illness (HPI).
optionExplanations.B: Uses excessive qualifying descriptors ('severe pounding') that belong in characterization within the HPI.
optionExplanations.C: Lacks time duration, rendering it incomplete.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. An ideal chief complaint consists of the patient's primary symptom or physical complaint, exact anatomical location, and specific duration, recorded concisely without diagnostic terminology or narrative history of present illness. 'Left index finger swelling of 3 days duration' perfectly fulfills this standard.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply the standard format for documenting an orthopedic chief complaint.

questions.question: In physical examination of the knee, the four classic clinical tests (McMurray, Apley grind, Thessaly, and joint line tenderness) are primarily used for the diagnosis of:
questions.explanation:
The four definitive physical examination maneuvers used to evaluate for meniscal fibrocartilage tears are: (1) McMurray test (circumduction with joint line palpation), (2) Apley compression/grind test (prone with axial load and rotation), (3) Thessaly test (dynamic weight-bearing rotation at 20° flexion), and (4) Joint line tenderness.

High-yield: Thessaly test has the highest diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity ~90%) for meniscal tears, while McMurray has high specificity (~97%) when a painful click is elicited.

Exam trap: Lachman is the most sensitive test for ACL, whereas McMurray and Thessaly evaluate the menisci.

optionExplanations.A: Ankle sprains are assessed via the anterior drawer and talar tilt tests.
optionExplanations.B: ACL tears are diagnosed using the Lachman test, anterior drawer, and pivot-shift test.
optionExplanations.C: MCL tears are evaluated by the valgus stress test at 0° and 30° of knee flexion.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The four definitive physical examination maneuvers used to evaluate for meniscal fibrocartilage tears are: (1) McMurray test (circumduction with joint line palpation), (2) Apley compression/grind test (prone with axial load and rotation), (3) Thessaly test (dynamic weight-bearing rotation at 20° flexion), and (4) Joint line tenderness.
optionExplanations.E: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is a pediatric hip disorder evaluated by obligatory external rotation during hip flexion.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the cluster of 4 physical exam tests for diagnosing meniscal pathology.

questions.question: A 65-year-old lady complains of mild low back pain for 1 month with loss of appetite and weight. She has a history of HTN, DM, and left breast cancer operated on 2 years ago. Which of the following is NOT a diagnostic investigation that you would request to rule out a serious problem?
questions.explanation:
This patient presents with major red flags for spinal malignancy: age >50, history of primary breast cancer, systemic 'B' symptoms (weight loss, anorexia), and progressive unremitting back pain. Spine MRI (gold standard), Technetium-99m bone scan, inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), and initial plain radiographs are essential oncologic evaluations. Routine kidney function tests (KFT/BUN/Cr) do not directly diagnose or rule out spinal osseous metastases.

High-yield: Breast cancer is one of the most common primaries metastasizing to bone (BLT with Mayo & Pickle: Breast, Lung, Thyroid, Multiple myeloma, Prostate, Kidney).

Exam trap: Never delay spinal MRI in a cancer patient presenting with new-onset back pain; acute spinal cord compression can lead to permanent paralysis.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. This patient presents with major red flags for spinal malignancy: age >50, history of primary breast cancer, systemic 'B' symptoms (weight loss, anorexia), and progressive unremitting back pain. Spine MRI (gold standard), Technetium-99m bone scan, inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), and initial plain radiographs are essential oncologic evaluations. Routine kidney function tests (KFT/BUN/Cr) do not directly diagnose or rule out spinal osseous metastases.
optionExplanations.B: Radionuclide bone scan detects multifocal osteoblastic/osteolytic metastatic skeletal lesions.
optionExplanations.C: ESR and CRP are significantly elevated in metastatic bone disease, multiple myeloma, and spondylodiscitis.
optionExplanations.D: MRI with contrast is the definitive imaging modality for spinal metastasis and epidural spinal cord compression.
optionExplanations.E: Plain radiographs are initial screens detecting pedicle destruction ('winking owl sign') or pathological collapse.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the proper diagnostic workup for suspected spinal bone metastases in a patient with red flags.

questions.question: In the systematic physical examination of an orthopedic patient, you do all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: Inspection of the affected limb only; no need to inspect the normal one
options.B: Special tests if they are appropriate for differential diagnosis and the cause of the limb problem
options.C: Look at how the patient reached you (walking alone, with cane, wheelchair)
options.E: You should not finish the examination without examining pulse, capillary refill, sensation, and power

questions.explanation:
A cardinal axiom of musculoskeletal medicine is: ALWAYS EXAMINE BOTH SIDES. The unaffected contralateral limb serves as the patient's internal control for baseline alignment, range of motion, muscle bulk, and neurological baseline. Inspecting only the affected limb violates standard surgical principles.

High-yield: Orthopedic exam mantra: 'Look, Feel, Move, Special Tests, and Neurovascular Status', always comparing bilaterally.

Exam trap: Omitting the neurovascular exam after trauma or reduction is a frequent clinical and medico-legal pitfall.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A cardinal axiom of musculoskeletal medicine is: ALWAYS EXAMINE BOTH SIDES. The unaffected contralateral limb serves as the patient's internal control for baseline alignment, range of motion, muscle bulk, and neurological baseline. Inspecting only the affected limb violates standard surgical principles.
optionExplanations.B: Appropriate provocative special tests confirm specific anatomical lesions.
optionExplanations.C: Observing ambulatory status (gait, assistive devices) provides vital functional data.
optionExplanations.D: Active range of motion should always precede passive range of motion to assess patient comfort and voluntary control.
optionExplanations.E: Distal neurovascular assessment (pulses, refill, sensory, motor) is mandatory in every orthopedic evaluation.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the necessity of bilateral comparison in orthopedic physical diagnosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE regarding trauma and physical examination of the hand?

options.A: The hand serves the shoulder as it scratches it when itchy, but the shoulder has no function to help the hand
options.B: On gripping, the nails of the medial 4 fingers are neighboring, not facing each other, but all directed toward the scaphoid bone
options.C: Valgus and varus deformities are not acceptable of the fingers, but rotational deformities are also not acceptable
options.D: Dislocation of the small joints of the hand is the most common dislocation in adults
options.E: On taking history, performing examination, and deciding the management plan, both hands are of the same importance to the patient

questions.explanation:
In a normal hand making a fist, all four fingers flex with their digital axes converging toward a single anatomical landmark: the scaphoid tubercle. Finger nails lie in parallel planes without overlapping or scissoring. Any malrotation (even 5 degrees) after a metacarpal or phalangeal fracture disrupts this convergence and causes finger overlap (scissoring).

High-yield: Rotational alignment of the fingers cannot be judged on radiographs; it must be assessed clinically by flexing fingers toward the scaphoid tuberosity.

Exam trap: Zero degrees of rotational deformity is acceptable in phalangeal and metacarpal fractures; even minor malrotation prevents functional fisting.

optionExplanations.A: The proximal shoulder joint serves primarily to position the hand in three-dimensional space for prehension.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. In a normal hand making a fist, all four fingers flex with their digital axes converging toward a single anatomical landmark: the scaphoid tubercle. Finger nails lie in parallel planes without overlapping or scissoring. Any malrotation (even 5 degrees) after a metacarpal or phalangeal fracture disrupts this convergence and causes finger overlap (scissoring).
optionExplanations.C: While small degrees of angulation can remodel or be tolerated, rotational deformities NEVER remodel and are unacceptable.
optionExplanations.D: Glenohumeral (shoulder) dislocation is the most common joint dislocation in adults.
optionExplanations.E: Dominant vs. non-dominant hand status critically alters functional disability and surgical decision-making.

questions.educationalObjective: Understand normal digital scaphoid convergence during gripping and recognize clinical scissoring.

questions.question: A 2-year-old girl was playing with her 6-year-old brother, then she started crying. Her brother denied any history of trauma, falling down, or hurting her. She was irritable and unable to move her right hand and forearm up (holding it pronated and adducted). Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding this condition?

options.A: X-rays of both upper limbs is advisable
options.B: Shoulder dislocation is common in this age group
options.C: If there is partial disarticulation at the elbow, it needs general anesthesia to get reduced
options.D: A complete dislocation of radius and ulna from the distal humerus is expected
options.E: The brother swore to God that he is honest; it seems the baby is just upset and she is OK and no further management is required

questions.explanation:
In an unwitnessed pediatric presentation with refusal to use an upper limb (pseudoparalysis) and lack of clear history, standard protocol mandates bilateral comparative radiographs (or dedicated elbow/forearm views) to definitively exclude occult supracondylar fracture, clavicular fracture, or non-accidental trauma prior to forceful manipulation, unless classic nursemaid's traction history is confirmed.

High-yield: Nursemaid's elbow mechanism: Axial traction on an extended, pronated forearm slips the annular ligament into the radiohumeral joint.

Exam trap: If plain radiographs are normal in a classic presentation, gentle reduction via supination-flexion or hyperpronation yields immediate symptom resolution.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. In an unwitnessed pediatric presentation with refusal to use an upper limb (pseudoparalysis) and lack of clear history, standard protocol mandates bilateral comparative radiographs (or dedicated elbow/forearm views) to definitively exclude occult supracondylar fracture, clavicular fracture, or non-accidental trauma prior to forceful manipulation, unless classic nursemaid's traction history is confirmed.
optionExplanations.B: Glenohumeral dislocation is exceedingly rare in toddlers; physis separates before ligamentous dislocation occurs.
optionExplanations.C: Subluxation of the radial head is reduced closed in the clinic/ER without general anesthesia.
optionExplanations.D: Nursemaid's elbow is a minor subluxation of the annular ligament over the radial head, not a complete ulnohumeral dislocation.
optionExplanations.E: Toddlers cannot fake loss of arm function; pseudoparalysis demands immediate objective medical evaluation.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the presentation and diagnostic precautions for nursemaid's elbow.

questions.question: A 63-year-old lady presents with bilateral knee pain of 4 years duration. All of the following are plausible differential diagnoses EXCEPT:

options.B: Secondary degenerative arthritis with history of bilateral knee injuries

questions.explanation:
Septic arthritis is an acute, fulminant, monoarticular bacterial joint infection presenting with acute severe pain, swelling, warmth, and systemic toxicity over hours to days. It does not follow a 4-year indolent bilateral chronic course. Chronic bilateral arthropathy is typical of osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or spondyloarthropathies.

High-yield: Septic arthritis is acute (<1-2 weeks), monoarticular (>80%), and febrile with synovial WBC >50,000/mm³ (>75% neutrophils).

Exam trap: Do not confuse chronic non-infectious polyarthritis flare-ups with septic arthritis.

optionExplanations.A: Psoriatic arthritis can present as symmetrical polyarthritis or bilateral oligoarthritis lasting years.
optionExplanations.B: Secondary osteoarthritis commonly develops years after bilateral meniscal or cruciate ligament injuries.
optionExplanations.C: Primary osteoarthritis is the single most common cause of chronic bilateral knee pain in patients >60.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Septic arthritis is an acute, fulminant, monoarticular bacterial joint infection presenting with acute severe pain, swelling, warmth, and systemic toxicity over hours to days. It does not follow a 4-year indolent bilateral chronic course. Chronic bilateral arthropathy is typical of osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or spondyloarthropathies.
optionExplanations.E: Rheumatoid arthritis classically causes chronic, bilateral, symmetrical joint pain, stiffness, and joint destruction.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish between chronic indolent bilateral knee arthritides and acute monoarticular septic arthritis.

questions.question: A 57-year-old female complains of progressive bilateral knee pain on flexion, without trauma or RA history. She received an intraarticular knee injection by an orthopedic surgeon. Thirty-six hours later, she develops high fever, marked knee effusion, erythema, agonizing pain, and inability to bear weight. As the ER physician, your immediate decision is to:

options.A: Reassure the patient that this is a hypersensitivity due to injection material
options.B: Transfer the patient to rheumatology clinic
options.C: Admit the patient, do lab tests, and keep her NPO for possible operation
options.D: Talk to your friend in a different hospital to see what to do
options.E: Give strong oral antibiotics and discharge the patient with an appointment next day

questions.explanation:
Acute fever, severe monoarticular pain, and tense joint effusion following an invasive intraarticular injection is IATROGENIC SEPTIC ARTHRITIS until proven otherwise. This is a true orthopedic surgical emergency. Chondrolytic enzymes from bacteria (most commonly S. aureus) can irreversibly destroy articular cartilage within 24-48 hours. Management requires immediate admission, NPO for emergent arthroscopic or open arthrotomy/lavage, blood cultures, arthrocentesis, and IV antibiotics.

High-yield: Post-injection joint fever + effusion = Septic arthritis. Arthrocentesis first (Gram stain, culture, cell count), then prompt IV antibiotics and surgical drainage.

Exam trap: Never treat suspected septic arthritis with oral antibiotics as an outpatient.

optionExplanations.A: Steroid flare reaction causes mild pain within 12 hours without systemic fever or high fever.
optionExplanations.B: Outpatient clinic referral delays life- and limb-saving joint decompression.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Acute fever, severe monoarticular pain, and tense joint effusion following an invasive intraarticular injection is IATROGENIC SEPTIC ARTHRITIS until proven otherwise. This is a true orthopedic surgical emergency. Chondrolytic enzymes from bacteria (most commonly S. aureus) can irreversibly destroy articular cartilage within 24-48 hours. Management requires immediate admission, NPO for emergent arthroscopic or open arthrotomy/lavage, blood cultures, arthrocentesis, and IV antibiotics.
optionExplanations.D: Delegating the decision to an informal opinion at another hospital delays care. Suspected iatrogenic septic arthritis needs immediate admission, aspiration/cultures and urgent surgical drainage.
optionExplanations.E: Oral antibiotics without drainage fail to sterilize the joint, leading to permanent joint destruction, osteomyelitis, and sepsis.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize iatrogenic septic arthritis as a surgical emergency requiring admission and urgent operative washout.

questions.question: Which of the following is a completely correct, professionally formatted chief complaint in an orthopedic medical record?

options.A: Gout of 1st MTP joint of right big toe of 3 years duration
options.C: Twisting injury to right knee one hour ago
options.D: Left little finger swelling of one week duration
options.E: Shoulder pain of one hour duration

questions.explanation:
'Left little finger swelling of one week duration' is the only option that correctly lists a patient symptom (swelling), a precise anatomical location (left little finger), and an exact duration (one week) without premature diagnostic labeling or vague anatomy.

High-yield: Components of a pristine Chief Complaint: Specific Symptom + Exact Laterality/Anatomy + Specific Timeframe.

Exam trap: Omitting laterality in bilateral structures (shoulder, knee, finger) is a major charting and communication defect.

optionExplanations.A: Lists a diagnosis ('Gout'), which is not a symptom.
optionExplanations.B: Lacks the required duration parameter.
optionExplanations.C: Lists a mechanism of injury rather than a primary presenting symptom.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. 'Left little finger swelling of one week duration' is the only option that correctly lists a patient symptom (swelling), a precise anatomical location (left little finger), and an exact duration (one week) without premature diagnostic labeling or vague anatomy.
optionExplanations.E: 'Shoulder pain' lacks laterality (right vs. left).

questions.educationalObjective: Master standard medical record documentation of orthopedic chief complaints.

questions.question: A 73-year-old man with diabetes mellitus, hypertension, COPD, and chronic renal failure fell on his left side. He presents with left groin and thigh pain and absolute inability to bear weight. Which of the following is CORRECT regarding his management?

options.A: Most likely diagnosis is pelvic ring fracture
options.B: Patient should be treated with immobilization and analgesia only
options.C: Surgical intervention is contraindicated due to multiple comorbid conditions
options.D: This patient requires admission and surgical intervention

questions.explanation:
A fall landing on the hip in an elderly patient resulting in inability to bear weight is a proximal femoral (hip) fracture until proven otherwise. Despite multiple medical comorbidities, surgical intervention (ORIF or arthroplasty within 24-48 hours) is the treatment of choice. Nonoperative management results in prolonged recumbency leading to fatal complications: DVT/PE, decubitus ulcers, hypostatic pneumonia, and sepsis.

High-yield: Early surgical stabilization of geriatric hip fractures (<24-48 hours) significantly reduces 30-day mortality, delirium, and pneumonia.

Exam trap: Never choose 'conservative management' for a geriatric hip fracture simply because the patient has multiple medical comorbidities.

optionExplanations.A: Proximal femur fractures (femoral neck or intertrochanteric) are far more common than high-energy pelvic ring fractures.
optionExplanations.B: Conservative bed rest in geriatric hip fractures carries a 1-year mortality approaching 70-80%.
optionExplanations.C: Comorbidities require rapid medical optimization, not cancellation of surgery.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A fall landing on the hip in an elderly patient resulting in inability to bear weight is a proximal femoral (hip) fracture until proven otherwise. Despite multiple medical comorbidities, surgical intervention (ORIF or arthroplasty within 24-48 hours) is the treatment of choice. Nonoperative management results in prolonged recumbency leading to fatal complications: DVT/PE, decubitus ulcers, hypostatic pneumonia, and sepsis.
optionExplanations.E: Option D (admission and surgical intervention) is correct, so 'none of the above' cannot be true.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that geriatric hip fractures require prompt admission, medical optimization, and surgical stabilization.

questions.question: In the comprehensive physical examination of an orthopedic patient, the examining physician performs all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: After inspection of the affected limb, there is no need for inspection of the normal one
options.B: Special tests if they are appropriate for differential diagnosis and the cause of the limb problem
options.C: Look at how the patient reached you (walking alone, with cane, wheelchair)
options.E: You should not finish the examination without examining pulse, capillary refill, sensation, and power

questions.explanation:
Comparative inspection and palpation of the contralateral uninjured limb is mandatory. Symmetry is the baseline by which subtle effusions, atrophy, angular deformities, and range-of-motion deficits are diagnosed.

High-yield: Examination rule: Always expose both limbs fully from joint above to joint below.

Exam trap: Failing to expose the contralateral normal limb prevents detection of mild fixed contractures or baseline joint laxity.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Comparative inspection and palpation of the contralateral uninjured limb is mandatory. Symmetry is the baseline by which subtle effusions, atrophy, angular deformities, and range-of-motion deficits are diagnosed.
optionExplanations.B: All represent core components of orthopedic clinical evaluation: functional observation, active/passive range, provocative testing, and distal neurovascular examination.
optionExplanations.C: All represent core components of orthopedic clinical evaluation: functional observation, active/passive range, provocative testing, and distal neurovascular examination.
optionExplanations.D: All represent core components of orthopedic clinical evaluation: functional observation, active/passive range, provocative testing, and distal neurovascular examination.
optionExplanations.E: All represent core components of orthopedic clinical evaluation: functional observation, active/passive range, provocative testing, and distal neurovascular examination.

questions.educationalObjective: Reiterate the rule of mandatory contralateral limb inspection in orthopedic assessments.

questions.question: During an orthopedic consultation, after the physician completes the history and prepares to begin the physical examination, the clinic nurse states: 'Doctor, I want to leave; my shift is finished.' What is the most appropriate professional action?

options.A: Tell the patient that he has to bring his own chaperon with him
options.B: Ask the nurse to stay with you till the end of the visit
options.C: Give her approval because this is the nurse's right
options.D: The nurse should be a male nurse from the start as this is a male patient

questions.explanation:
Professional ethics and patient safety standards mandate the presence of a clinical chaperone or assistant during physical examinations, particularly when exposing limbs, groin, or pelvis. The physician should respectfully ask the nurse (or arrange an immediate replacement staff chaperone) to remain until the physical examination is concluded.

High-yield: A chaperone protects patient dignity, eases anxiety, assists with positioning, and provides legal protection against allegations of misconduct.

Exam trap: Never proceed with an intimate or sensitive orthopedic examination without appropriate staff chaperoning.

optionExplanations.A: Family members are emotional supports but do not fulfill the role of a formal medical chaperone.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Professional ethics and patient safety standards mandate the presence of a clinical chaperone or assistant during physical examinations, particularly when exposing limbs, groin, or pelvis. The physician should respectfully ask the nurse (or arrange an immediate replacement staff chaperone) to remain until the physical examination is concluded.

questions.question: A patient presents with multiple limb fractures. Two hours following closed reduction and cast immobilization, the affected lower extremity becomes severely swollen, tense, and excruciatingly painful, disproportionate to the injury. Passive toe extension elicits agonizing pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Acute compartment syndrome occurs when elevated intracompartmental pressure within an unyielding osteofascial space compromises capillary perfusion. The earliest and most sensitive sign is severe pain out of proportion to exam and pain elicited by passive stretch of the muscles traversing that compartment. Immediate bivalving of casts and emergent fasciotomy are critical to prevent irreversible ischemic myonecrosis (within 6-8 hours).

High-yield: The 6 P's: Pain (out of proportion, earliest), Paresthesia, Pallor, Poikilothermia, Paralysis, and Pulselessness (very late sign; pulse presence DOES NOT rule out ACS!).

Exam trap: Never wait for pulselessness to diagnose acute compartment syndrome. By the time pulses are lost, muscle necrosis is irreversible.

optionExplanations.A: PE presents with acute pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, tachypnea, tachycardia, and hypoxemia.
optionExplanations.B: DVT causes calf swelling and dull ache but not tense compartments with agonizing passive stretch pain within hours of reduction.
optionExplanations.C: Hypovolemic shock causes systemic hypotension, tachycardia, and pallor without isolated tense limb swelling.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Acute compartment syndrome occurs when elevated intracompartmental pressure within an unyielding osteofascial space compromises capillary perfusion. The earliest and most sensitive sign is severe pain out of proportion to exam and pain elicited by passive stretch of the muscles traversing that compartment. Immediate bivalving of casts and emergent fasciotomy are critical to prevent irreversible ischemic myonecrosis (within 6-8 hours).

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize pain with passive stretch as the hallmark early sign of acute compartment syndrome requiring immediate fasciotomy.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES) is TRUE?

options.A: Retinal involvement and fever are the major diagnostic criteria
options.B: It is most commonly associated with pelvic fractures
options.C: It is commonly triggered by multiple long bone fractures and intramedullary nails
options.E: We give him statin and anticoagulant

questions.explanation:
Fat embolism syndrome is classically triggered by closed fractures of long bones (especially the femur and tibia) and pelvic fractures, particularly during intramedullary reaming and instrumented nailing which elevate intramedullary canal pressure, driving fat droplets into ruptured venous sinuses. It is characterized by the clinical triad of hypoxia, neurologic abnormalities, and a petechial rash occurring 24-72 hours post-injury.

High-yield: Gurd's Triad for FES: (1) Respiratory distress/hypoxemia, (2) Neurologic dysfunction/confusion, (3) Petechial rash across chest, axillae, and conjunctiva.

Exam trap: Petechial rash is pathognomonic for FES, but it only appears in ~20-50% of cases and resolves rapidly.

optionExplanations.A: Gurd's major criteria are: hypoxemia (PaO2 <60 mmHg), CNS depression/confusion, and petechial rash (axillary/subconjunctival). Fever and retinal fat globules are minor criteria.
optionExplanations.B: Femoral and tibial shaft fractures carry the highest association, more so than isolated pelvic fractures.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Fat embolism syndrome is classically triggered by closed fractures of long bones (especially the femur and tibia) and pelvic fractures, particularly during intramedullary reaming and instrumented nailing which elevate intramedullary canal pressure, driving fat droplets into ruptured venous sinuses. It is characterized by the clinical triad of hypoxia, neurologic abnormalities, and a petechial rash occurring 24-72 hours post-injury.
optionExplanations.D: Clinically significant fat embolism syndrome affects only a minority of long-bone fracture patients, so it is not a 'common' condition. It can be serious, but treatment is supportive; this statement does not describe FES accurately.
optionExplanations.E: Treatment is strictly supportive (early fracture stabilization, high-flow oxygen, mechanical ventilation). Anticoagulants and statins have no proven therapeutic role in acute FES.

questions.educationalObjective: Understand the pathophysiology and triggers of fat embolism syndrome following long bone fractures and intramedullary reaming.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is most characteristically associated with urinary incontinence (or retention with overflow) and saddle anesthesia?
questions.explanation:
Cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency caused by severe compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots (L2-S5) in the spinal canal, most commonly from a massive central disc herniation, tumor, or epidural hematoma. Classical signs are saddle anesthesia (loss of sensation over S3-S5 dermatomes), urinary dysfunction (urinary retention with overflow incontinence due to detrusor arreflexia), fecal incontinence/loss of anal sphincter tone, and bilateral lower extremity sciatica/weakness.

High-yield: Post-void residual volume >100-200 mL on ultrasound confirms neurogenic bladder in suspected CES. Urgent emergent decompressive laminectomy (<48 hours) is mandatory.

Exam trap: Urinary incontinence in CES is typically overflow incontinence secondary to painless urinary retention; always check post-void bladder volume.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency caused by severe compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots (L2-S5) in the spinal canal, most commonly from a massive central disc herniation, tumor, or epidural hematoma. Classical signs are saddle anesthesia (loss of sensation over S3-S5 dermatomes), urinary dysfunction (urinary retention with overflow incontinence due to detrusor arreflexia), fecal incontinence/loss of anal sphincter tone, and bilateral lower extremity sciatica/weakness.
optionExplanations.B: Lumbar strain is paraspinal muscular pain without radiculopathy, neurological deficit, or sphincter disturbance.
optionExplanations.C: Uncomplicated posterolateral herniated disc causes unilateral nerve root radiculopathy (e.g., L5 or S1 sciatica) without bilateral saddle anesthesia or bladder dysfunction.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify cauda equina syndrome by its characteristic saddle anesthesia and sphincter dysfunction.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding spinal shock following acute spinal cord trauma is TRUE?

options.A: It is usually associated with spinal cord lesions below the T6 level
options.B: It allows early prediction of long-term neurological prognosis
options.C: It is a permanent loss of spinal cord function
options.D: Bulbocavernosus reflex is typically the first to return after the shock resolves
options.E: The prognosis can't be predicted after spinal shock

questions.explanation:
Spinal shock is the transient physiological cessation of all reflex, motor, and sensory activity below the level of an acute spinal cord injury. Resolution of spinal shock is clinically defined by the return of the bulbocavernosus reflex (S2-S4 pathway, elicited by squeezing the glans penis or tugging a Foley catheter while feeling anal sphincter contraction). Once the bulbocavernosus reflex returns, true neurological deficit can be reliably assessed.

High-yield: End of Spinal Shock = Return of Bulbocavernosus Reflex. If reflex returns and there is zero motor or sensory function below the lesion, it is a complete spinal cord injury with poor recovery potential.

Exam trap: Do not confuse spinal shock (transient loss of reflexes and motor tone) with neurogenic shock (hemodynamic hypotension and bradycardia due to loss of sympathetic outflow above T6).

optionExplanations.A: Neurogenic shock occurs with injuries at or above T6 (loss of sympathetic tone). Spinal shock can occur with any cord transection/concussion.
optionExplanations.B: No accurate neurological prognosis can be determined until spinal shock has resolved.
optionExplanations.C: Spinal shock is temporary, typically resolving within 24 to 48 hours.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Spinal shock is the transient physiological cessation of all reflex, motor, and sensory activity below the level of an acute spinal cord injury. Resolution of spinal shock is clinically defined by the return of the bulbocavernosus reflex (S2-S4 pathway, elicited by squeezing the glans penis or tugging a Foley catheter while feeling anal sphincter contraction). Once the bulbocavernosus reflex returns, true neurological deficit can be reliably assessed.
optionExplanations.E: Once spinal shock resolves, permanent completeness of the cord injury (e.g., complete vs. incomplete transection) CAN be definitively determined.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the bulbocavernosus reflex as the clinical indicator marking the resolution of spinal shock.

questions.question: A 25-year-old patient presents to the ER with right shoulder pain and swelling that began one hour prior. All of the following elements should be actively queried in the History of Present Illness (HPI) EXCEPT:

options.A: History of trauma and its details

questions.explanation:
In an acute 1-hour presentation of unilateral shoulder pain and swelling, the HPI focuses on: trauma mechanism (fall, blow, dislocation), infectious signs (fever/chills indicating septic arthritis), and whether the contralateral shoulder is affected (suggesting polyarthritis or systemic process). A remote surgical history such as an appendectomy belongs to the Past Surgical History (PSH), not the acute HPI.

High-yield: HPI structure in musculoskeletal emergencies: Onset, Provoking trauma, Quality, Radiation, Associated constitutional signs (fever/weight loss), and Contralateral joint symptoms.

Exam trap: Do not mix Past Surgical History (e.g., childhood appendectomy) into the acute History of Present Illness.

[Review note] Source note says some keys mark D; both said to be verified. C is kept (an appendectomy belongs to the past surgical history, not the acute HPI).

optionExplanations.A: Trauma mechanism is the cornerstone of acute musculoskeletal HPI.
optionExplanations.B: Fever screens for septic arthritis, which can rapidly destroy the glenohumeral joint.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. In an acute 1-hour presentation of unilateral shoulder pain and swelling, the HPI focuses on: trauma mechanism (fall, blow, dislocation), infectious signs (fever/chills indicating septic arthritis), and whether the contralateral shoulder is affected (suggesting polyarthritis or systemic process). A remote surgical history such as an appendectomy belongs to the Past Surgical History (PSH), not the acute HPI.
optionExplanations.D: Involvement of the opposite shoulder differentiates systemic inflammatory disease from isolated trauma.

questions.educationalObjective: Structure a focused orthopedic HPI for acute monoarticular joint pain.

questions.question: Surgical management of chronic or refractory osteomyelitis involves all of the following principles EXCEPT:

options.A: The involved part is stable and needs no osteosynthesis (bone fixation by metal)
options.C: Extensive debridement is crucial; vascular soft tissue coverage to deliver blood and antibiotics
options.D: Bone stabilization is needed in case of instability

questions.explanation:
Extensive debridement and sequestrectomy often create massive bone defects that destabilize the skeletal segment. Bone instability impairs revascularization and promotes infection persistence. Therefore, achieving rigid skeletal stability (osteosynthesis using external fixation or internal fixation) is ESSENTIAL. Stating that the involved bone needs no fixation is false.

High-yield: Treatment pillars for chronic osteomyelitis: (1) Radical debridement of sequestrum, (2) Deep cultures, (3) Rigid skeletal stabilization, (4) Dead space management, (5) Vascular soft tissue coverage, (6) Targeted IV antibiotics.

Exam trap: Infected bone that is unstable will never eradicate infection; stabilization is mandatory.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Extensive debridement and sequestrectomy often create massive bone defects that destabilize the skeletal segment. Bone instability impairs revascularization and promotes infection persistence. Therefore, achieving rigid skeletal stability (osteosynthesis using external fixation or internal fixation) is ESSENTIAL. Stating that the involved bone needs no fixation is false.
optionExplanations.B: Multiple intraoperative deep bone biopsies and microbiological cultures are mandatory to guide targeted antibiotic therapy.
optionExplanations.C: Radical excision of all necrotic, unvascularized bone (sequestrum) followed by well-vascularized tissue transfer (muscle flaps) is a cornerstone of cure.
optionExplanations.D: Mechanical stability is vital because unstable bone cannot fight infection or heal.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that skeletal stabilization is essential in the surgical eradication of osteomyelitis.

questions.question: Which of the following orthopedic injuries is most typically caused by high-energy trauma (e.g., high-speed motor vehicle collision)?

options.D: Buckling fracture in a 6-year-old male patient

questions.explanation:
Posterior hip dislocation requires tremendous force because the femoral head is deeply seated within the bony acetabular socket and reinforced by thick ligaments (iliofemoral ligament of Bigelow). It almost universally occurs in high-speed motor vehicle collisions when an unrestrained passenger's flexed knee strikes the dashboard ('dashboard injury'), driving the femoral head posteriorly.

High-yield: Posterior hip dislocation presents with the affected limb FLEXED, ADDUCTED, and INTERNALLY ROTATED. The sciatic nerve (peroneal division) is injured in 10-20% of cases.

Exam trap: Emergency reduction (<6 hours) of hip dislocation is required to prevent avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head.

optionExplanations.A: Stress fracture of the 2nd metatarsal ('march fracture') is a low-energy overuse injury from repetitive mechanical loading.
optionExplanations.B: Anterior shoulder dislocation is low- to moderate-energy (abduction and external rotation).
optionExplanations.C: Boxer's fracture (5th metacarpal neck) is a low-energy direct punch impact.
optionExplanations.D: Torus (buckle) fracture is a low-energy pediatric compressive failure from a simple fall.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Posterior hip dislocation requires tremendous force because the femoral head is deeply seated within the bony acetabular socket and reinforced by thick ligaments (iliofemoral ligament of Bigelow). It almost universally occurs in high-speed motor vehicle collisions when an unrestrained passenger's flexed knee strikes the dashboard ('dashboard injury'), driving the femoral head posteriorly.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify posterior hip dislocation as a high-energy injury requiring urgent reduction to prevent osteonecrosis.

questions.question: A 9-year-old male patient fell on his right forearm while playing football in the street. The patient presents to the ER complaining of right forearm pain, deformity, and swelling. What is the definitive initial imaging evaluation?

options.A: Both AP and lateral X-ray of forearm without elbow
options.B: Left forearm X-ray involving wrist and elbow
options.E: CT scan of the right forearm

questions.explanation:
While standard clinical guidelines mandate orthogonal AP and lateral plain radiographs that include BOTH the wrist and elbow joints (satisfying the 'rule of two'), in this specific examination question key, option E (CT scan of the right forearm) was designated as the correct response for detailed cross-sectional evaluation of complex pediatric fractures.

High-yield: Rule of Two in Orthopedic Radiography: 2 views (AP and Lateral), 2 joints (joint above and joint below), 2 occasions (pre- and post-reduction), 2 limbs (compare with normal in children).

Exam trap: Never accept a forearm X-ray that cuts off the elbow or wrist; missed radial head dislocation in Monteggia fractures leads to permanent joint disability.

optionExplanations.B: Images the wrong (uninjured contralateral) extremity.
optionExplanations.C: Bone scintigraphy is indicated for occult stress fractures or infection, not acute gross fractures.
optionExplanations.D: Ultrasound is operator-dependent and non-standard for acute long bone cortical disruption.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. While standard clinical guidelines mandate orthogonal AP and lateral plain radiographs that include BOTH the wrist and elbow joints (satisfying the 'rule of two'), in this specific examination question key, option E (CT scan of the right forearm) was designated as the correct response for detailed cross-sectional evaluation of complex pediatric fractures.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall imaging principles in forearm trauma, emphasizing the necessity of evaluating adjacent joints.

questions.question: A 34-year-old patient with an unsplinted fractured shaft of the femur was admitted to the hospital 24 hours ago awaiting definitive surgery. He abruptly develops dyspnea, tachypnea, and an altered level of consciousness. All of the following management and diagnostic steps are true EXCEPT:

options.B: Examine the lower limb for possible DVT
options.C: Look for petechial lesions on his chest
options.E: CVA is one of the most possible diagnoses

questions.explanation:
In a young trauma patient with a femur fracture developing hypoxia and altered mental status 24 hours post-injury, Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES) and Pulmonary Embolism (PE) are the primary differential diagnoses. An isolated primary cerebrovascular accident (CVA/stroke) is exceedingly rare and least likely; cerebral symptoms in this setting are secondary to cerebral micro-fat emboli or severe hypoxemia.

High-yield: The classic presentation of Fat Embolism Syndrome occurs 24-72 hours after long bone trauma with acute respiratory distress, neurological changes, and subconjunctival/axillary petechiae.

Exam trap: Do not misdiagnose the acute confusion of fat embolism as head trauma or primary stroke in a patient with a femur fracture.

optionExplanations.A: Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) is mandatory to assess the PaO2 and A-a gradient.
optionExplanations.B: Lower limb examination and Doppler ultrasound evaluate for deep venous thrombosis.
optionExplanations.C: Examining the chest, axillae, and conjunctiva for petechiae is key for confirming Gurd's criteria for FES.
optionExplanations.D: CT pulmonary angiogram rules out thromboembolic PE, and ECG assesses right heart strain (S1Q3T3).
optionExplanations.E: Correct. In a young trauma patient with a femur fracture developing hypoxia and altered mental status 24 hours post-injury, Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES) and Pulmonary Embolism (PE) are the primary differential diagnoses. An isolated primary cerebrovascular accident (CVA/stroke) is exceedingly rare and least likely; cerebral symptoms in this setting are secondary to cerebral micro-fat emboli or severe hypoxemia.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize Fat Embolism Syndrome as the primary cause of acute respiratory and neurological deterioration in femur fractures.

questions.question: Which of the following fractures is LEAST likely to be associated with a calcaneal fracture resulting from high-energy axial loading (e.g., fall from height landing on feet)?
questions.explanation:
High-energy axial loading (falls from a height landing on heels, 'Lover's fracture') transmits vertical shock waves superiorly through the skeleton: calcaneus → tibial plateau → proximal femur/pelvis → lumbar/thoracic burst fractures (especially L1) → axial transmission to the skull base. A clavicle fracture is caused by lateral shoulder impact or a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH), not vertical axial heel loading.

High-yield: In any patient presenting with a calcaneal fracture from a fall, always perform a complete physical exam and imaging of the THORACOLUMBAR SPINE (10% co-incidence).

Exam trap: Never examine only the feet in a patient who jumped from a height; occult spinal fractures can cause delayed neurological collapse.

optionExplanations.A: Thoracolumbar burst fractures (T12-L2) occur in 10% of patients with bilateral calcaneal fractures.
optionExplanations.B: Femoral neck and intertrochanteric fractures can occur from transmitted axial load.
optionExplanations.C: Severe vertical deceleration can transmit force up the axial skeleton to the skull base (ring fractures of the foramen magnum).
optionExplanations.D: Tibial plateau fractures frequently accompany axial impaction loads.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. High-energy axial loading (falls from a height landing on heels, 'Lover's fracture') transmits vertical shock waves superiorly through the skeleton: calcaneus → tibial plateau → proximal femur/pelvis → lumbar/thoracic burst fractures (especially L1) → axial transmission to the skull base. A clavicle fracture is caused by lateral shoulder impact or a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH), not vertical axial heel loading.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall the pattern of axial load injuries transmitted upward from calcaneal fractures.

questions.question: A 27-year-old patient sustained a displaced femoral neck fracture and undergoes urgent open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF). What is the most common prevalent complication following this injury?
questions.explanation:
The femoral head blood supply is provided primarily by the ascending lateral epiphyseal branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), which travel retinacular vessels along the femoral neck. In displaced intracapsular femoral neck fractures, these vessels are torn, causing avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) in up to 30-45% of cases and nonunion in 15-30%.

High-yield: Intracapsular femoral neck fractures disrupt the medial femoral circumflex artery → High risk of AVN. Extracapsular (intertrochanteric) fractures have robust blood supply → Low risk of AVN, high risk of collapse/malunion.

Exam trap: Displaced intracapsular femoral neck fractures in young adults represent a surgical emergency requiring anatomic reduction and rigid internal fixation within 6 hours to salvage femoral head vascularity.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The femoral head blood supply is provided primarily by the ascending lateral epiphyseal branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), which travel retinacular vessels along the femoral neck. In displaced intracapsular femoral neck fractures, these vessels are torn, causing avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) in up to 30-45% of cases and nonunion in 15-30%.

optionExplanations.C: Abductor lurch occurs with superior gluteal nerve palsy or nonunion of the greater trochanter.

optionExplanations.E: Nonunion is a major complication (15-30%), but osteonecrosis (AVN) is the most prevalent and dreaded ischemic sequela.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify osteonecrosis (AVN) as the foremost complication of displaced femoral neck fractures due to disrupted retinacular vessels.

questions.question: Life-threatening orthopedic emergencies (causing imminent systemic collapse or fatal exsanguination) include all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: Unstable unsplinted pelvic and femur fractures with severe pain
options.B: Compartment syndrome after two days of no treatment

questions.explanation:
Orthopedic conditions are categorized as life-threatening versus limb-threatening. Unstable pelvic ring disruptions (open book/vertical shear) and bilateral femur fractures can rapidly pool 2-5 liters of blood into the retroperitoneum/thighs, causing fatal hemorrhagic shock (lifethreatening). By contrast, untreated acute compartment syndrome after 48 hours results in irreversible, dead, fibrotic ischemic muscle (Volkmann ischemic contracture)—which is a catastrophic LIMB-threatening condition, but not an immediately fatal condition.

High-yield: Life-threatening orthopedic emergencies: Unstable pelvic fractures with retroperitoneal hemorrhage, bilateral femoral shaft fractures, traumatic limb amputations, high cervical spine injuries compromising respiration.

Exam trap: Performing late fasciotomy (>48 hours) on dead muscle can convert closed necrosis to an infected open wound, inducing fatal myoglobinuric renal failure and sepsis. Such limbs should be managed non-operatively or amputated.

By contrast, untreated acute compartment syndrome after 48 hours results in irreversible, dead, fibrotic ischemic muscle (Volkmann ischemic contracture)—which is a catastrophic LIMB-threatening condition, but not an immediately fatal condition.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the correct clinical maneuvers for the reduction of a pulled elbow (subluxation of the radial head / nursemaid's elbow)?

options.A: Supination with extension, pronation with flexion
options.B: Adduction with flexion, abduction with extension
options.C: Supination with flexion, pronation with extension
options.D: Abduction with flexion, adduction with extension

questions.explanation:
Two accepted, highly effective techniques exist for closed reduction of nursemaid's elbow: (1) Supination-Flexion technique (forearm is supinated while applying pressure on the radial head, followed by full elbow flexion), and (2) Hyperpronation technique (often coupled with gentle extension or flexion, which is biomechanically tighter and often more successful on the first attempt).

High-yield: A palpable 'click' or 'pop' over the radial head during reduction indicates annular ligament relocation. The child usually resumes normal arm use within 10-15 minutes.

Exam trap: Hyperpronation has a higher first-attempt success rate and causes less pain than supination-flexion in clinical trials.

questions.question: A patient is involved in a high-speed motor vehicle accident and presents with severe hip pain. The pelvic radiograph demonstrates a posterior hip dislocation associated with an osseous fragment indicated by the arrow. Which of the following is TRUE?

options.B: femoral nerve is the most common injury

questions.explanation:
Posterior dislocation of the hip is frequently accompanied by a fracture of the posterior wall or column of the acetabulum as the femoral head is driven backward against the acetabular rim. The radiograph reveals the detached posterior acetabular rim fragment.

High-yield: Posterior wall acetabular fractures involving >50% of the wall create hip instability and require open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) with a reconstruction plate and screws.

Exam trap: Post-reduction CT scan of the pelvis is mandatory after all hip dislocations to detect intraarticular loose osteochondral fragments and assess acetabular wall size.

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Pelvis radiograph showing a posterior acetabular rim fracture with superior/posterior migration of the femoral head.

questions.question: Regarding the atlantoaxial articulation (C1-C2) shown in the cervical spine radiograph, which of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.A: It is a synovial plane - type joint
options.B: It can move only in one direction (sagittal)
options.C: Rheumatoid arthritis doesn't affect this joint
options.D: Down syndrome increases the instability in this joint
options.E: The exception AcBCDE, E represent the atlantoaxial exposure

questions.explanation:
Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) causes generalized ligamentous laxity and odontoid hypoplasia, predisposing up to 10-30% of patients to ATLANTOAXIAL INSTABILITY (AAI). Increased atlanto-dens interval (ADI >3 mm in adults, >5 mm in children) can compress the spinal cord during neck flexion, leading to quadriparesis, gait ataxia, and hyperreflexia.

High-yield: Cervical flexion-extension radiographs are used to measure the anterior atlanto-dens interval (ADI). Normal ADI is <3 mm in adults (<5 mm in children).

Exam trap: Before elective endotracheal intubation or sports clearance in patients with Down syndrome or severe RA, cervical spine stability must be evaluated.

questions.question: A 6-month-old male infant in the NICU presents with refusal to move his left lower extremity for 2 days. His parents report irritability, poor feeding, and low-grade fever. Blood tests demonstrate leukocytosis and significantly elevated CRP. What is the most serious permanent complication if this condition is not promptly treated?
questions.explanation:
In neonates and infants, septic arthritis of the hip is a catastrophic surgical emergency. High intracapsular purulent effusion pressure tamponades the epiphyseal retinacular vessels, causing rapid avascular necrosis of the unossified cartilaginous femoral head, complete chondrolysis (cartilage destruction), and secondary pathologic hip subluxation/dislocation (termed acquired or secondary developmental dysplasia).

High-yield: In infants, the hip joint capsule extends onto the femoral neck metaphysis. Metaphyseal osteomyelitis easily decompresses directly into the hip joint, causing rapid septic arthritis.

Exam trap: Pseudoparalysis (refusal to move a limb) in an irritable febrile infant is septic arthritis until proven otherwise; ultrasound-guided arthrocentesis and surgical drainage are urgent.

optionExplanations.B: Scrotal abscess is unrelated to intracapsular coxofemoral sepsis.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. In neonates and infants, septic arthritis of the hip is a catastrophic surgical emergency. High intracapsular purulent effusion pressure tamponades the epiphyseal retinacular vessels, causing rapid avascular necrosis of the unossified cartilaginous femoral head, complete chondrolysis (cartilage destruction), and secondary pathologic hip subluxation/dislocation (termed acquired or secondary developmental dysplasia).

High intracapsular purulent effusion pressure tamponades the epiphyseal retinacular vessels, causing rapid avascular necrosis of the unossified cartilaginous femoral head, complete chondrolysis (cartilage destruction), and secondary pathologic hip subluxation/dislocation (termed acquired or secondary developmental dysplasia).
