questions.question: A 40-year-old utility worker suffered an electrical shock and presents with severe right shoulder pain, adducted and internally rotated arm posture, and inability to externally rotate. Initial AP radiographs appear inconclusive. What is the most appropriate imaging study to order next to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Violent muscle contractions caused by electrical shock or grand mal seizures disproportionately overpower internal rotators (latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major, subscapularis) relative to external rotators, forcing the humeral head posteriorly. Posterior dislocations are missed on up to 50-70% of standard AP X-rays. A CT scan (or axillary/Velpeau view) definitively demonstrates posterior glenohumeral translation and reverse Hill-Sachs lesions.

High-yield: Posterior shoulder dislocation classic triggers: '3 E's' - Electrocution, Epilepsy (seizures), and Extreme trauma. Clinical sign: Fixed internal rotation with loss of external rotation.

Exam trap: AP radiograph findings of posterior dislocation are subtle: 'lightbulb sign' (symmetric round humeral head due to internal rotation) and 'rim sign' (>6 mm joint space).

[Review note] Source key is B (CT). The axillary view (option D) is the standard next plain-film study; CT is definitive. Source key retained.

optionExplanations.A: Standard chest/arm lateral views do not profile the glenohumeral articulation clearly.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Violent muscle contractions caused by electrical shock or grand mal seizures disproportionately overpower internal rotators (latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major, subscapularis) relative to external rotators, forcing the humeral head posteriorly. Posterior dislocations are missed on up to 50-70% of standard AP X-rays. A CT scan (or axillary/Velpeau view) definitively demonstrates posterior glenohumeral translation and reverse Hill-Sachs lesions.
optionExplanations.C: MRI is sensitive for labral tears but is slow, expensive, and unnecessary for bony alignment in acute trauma.
optionExplanations.D: Axillary plain radiograph is an excellent orthogonal view, but when plain films are equivocal or pain prevents arm abduction, CT scan provides 100% sensitivity.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify electrical injury and seizures as triggers for posterior shoulder dislocation, requiring CT or axillary views for confirmation.

questions.question: The physical examination finding demonstrating flexion at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint and hyperextension at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint is known as:
questions.explanation:
Boutonnière deformity is characterized by PIP joint flexion and DIP joint hyperextension. The primary anatomical lesion is disruption or attenuation of the central slip of the extensor digitorum tendon over the PIP joint. This allows the lateral bands to sublux volar to the PIP flexion-extension axis, transforming them from PIP extensors into paradoxical PIP flexors, while exerting excessive extensor tension across the DIP joint.

High-yield: Boutonnière: PIP Flexed, DIP Extended (Central slip rupture + volar migration of lateral bands). Swan Neck: PIP Extended, DIP Flexed (Volar plate laxity + terminal tendon stretch).

Exam trap: Do not confuse Boutonnière deformity with Mallet finger (isolated DIP flexion due to terminal extensor tendon avulsion).

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Clinical photograph of a digit showing classic PIP flexion with compensatory DIP hyperextension.

optionExplanations.A: Claw finger (intrinsic minus) involves MCP hyperextension and flexion of both PIP and DIP joints, seen in ulnar nerve palsy.
optionExplanations.B: The 'OK sign' tests anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) function (FPL and FDP index).
optionExplanations.C: Swan neck deformity is the exact reciprocal: PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Boutonnière deformity is characterized by PIP joint flexion and DIP joint hyperextension. The primary anatomical lesion is disruption or attenuation of the central slip of the extensor digitorum tendon over the PIP joint. This allows the lateral bands to sublux volar to the PIP flexion-extension axis, transforming them from PIP extensors into paradoxical PIP flexors, while exerting excessive extensor tension across the DIP joint.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate Boutonnière deformity from Swan neck and Mallet finger deformities.

questions.question: The digit deformity characterized by hyperextension at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint and flexion at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint is designated as:
questions.explanation:
Swan neck deformity is characterized by hyperextension of the PIP joint and flexion of the DIP joint. It occurs when there is attenuation or rupture of the volar plate at the PIP joint (common in Rheumatoid Arthritis) or secondary to untreated mallet finger (extensor overpull on the PIP). The lateral bands displace dorsal to the PIP flexion-extension axis, locking the PIP in hyperextension.

High-yield: In Rheumatoid Arthritis: Boutonnière begins at the central slip; Swan neck begins at the volar plate or terminal tendon. Both impair prehension and functional grasp.

Exam trap: Silver ring splints can be used conservatively to prevent PIP hyperextension in flexible swan neck deformities.

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Clinical photograph showing hyperextension at the PIP joint and secondary flexion at the DIP joint of the index finger.

optionExplanations.A: Boutonnière features PIP flexion and DIP extension.
optionExplanations.B: Hammer toe is a pedal deformity featuring PIP flexion, MTP extension, and DIP extension/neutral.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Swan neck deformity is characterized by hyperextension of the PIP joint and flexion of the DIP joint. It occurs when there is attenuation or rupture of the volar plate at the PIP joint (common in Rheumatoid Arthritis) or secondary to untreated mallet finger (extensor overpull on the PIP). The lateral bands displace dorsal to the PIP flexion-extension axis, locking the PIP in hyperextension.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the anatomical posture and pathophysiology of Swan neck deformity.

questions.question: All of the following general statements regarding joints and articulations are true EXCEPT:

options.A: A joint is an articulation between two bones
options.B: Disruption of a pivot joint is one of rheumatoid arthritis problems
options.C: The ankle joint is a hinge joint
options.D: Any joint can be ball & socket, fibrous, or cartilaginous
options.E: A condyloid joint does not rotate like a ball & socket joint

questions.explanation:
Joints are classified structurally into three distinct primary categories: Fibrous (synarthroses), Cartilaginous (amphiarthroses), and Synovial (diarthroses). 'Ball and socket' (spheroidal) is a specific morphological subtype of Synovial joints, not an interchangeable primary class alongside fibrous and cartilaginous.

High-yield: Structural joint classification: (1) Synovial (diarthrodial: plane, hinge, pivot, condyloid, saddle, ball & socket), (2) Cartilaginous (synchondroses, symphyses), (3) Fibrous (sutures, gomphoses, syndesmoses).

Exam trap: Remember that only ball-and-socket joints permit multi-axial movement including full rotation.

optionExplanations.A: Definition of an anatomical joint is an articulation between two or more bones.
optionExplanations.B: Rheumatoid arthritis targets the median atlantoaxial joint, which is a synovial pivot joint.
optionExplanations.C: The talocrural (ankle) joint is functionally a uniaxial hinge (ginglymus) joint facilitating dorsiflexion and plantarflexion.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Joints are classified structurally into three distinct primary categories: Fibrous (synarthroses), Cartilaginous (amphiarthroses), and Synovial (diarthroses). 'Ball and socket' (spheroidal) is a specific morphological subtype of Synovial joints, not an interchangeable primary class alongside fibrous and cartilaginous.
optionExplanations.E: Condyloid (ellipsoidal) joints (e.g., radiocarpal, MCP) allow biaxial flexion-extension and abduction-adduction, but NOT axial rotation.

questions.educationalObjective: Understand the structural and functional classification schemes of human joints.

questions.question: Which of the following describes the correct pathophysiological pathway leading to long-term joint disability following an unreduced or severe joint dislocation?

options.A: Dislocation → Chondrolysis by special microorganisms → Healing by fibrosis
options.C: Dislocation → Avascular necrosis → Bone is healed by fibrous tissue which is not good bone
options.D: Dislocation → Subluxation → Displaced fracture → Deformity → Disability
options.E: Dislocation → Avascular necrosis below cartilage → Stresses on cartilage → Irreversible cartilage wear

questions.explanation:
Severe joint dislocation tears the capsular and periarticular arterial supplies (e.g., circumflex vessels in the hip or shoulder). This produces subchondral avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) in the bone underlying the articular cartilage. Dead subchondral bone undergoes microfractures and mechanical collapse under weight-bearing stresses, leading to incongruity, shear stresses across the articular surface, and irreversible cartilage wear (secondary post-traumatic osteoarthritis).

High-yield: Avascular necrosis primarily compromises the structural support of the overlying hyaline cartilage, precipitating chondral delamination and secondary joint osteoarthritis.

Exam trap: Even if joint alignment is restored, delayed reduction dramatically increases the risk of irreversible subchondral necrosis.

optionExplanations.A: Dislocation is a mechanical insult; bacterial chondrolysis occurs only in septic arthritis.
optionExplanations.B: Nerve injury can occur, but progressive joint destruction is fundamentally driven by cartilage and bony mechanical breakdown.
optionExplanations.C: Do not accurately capture the subchondral collapse and cartilage wear mechanism.
optionExplanations.D: Do not accurately capture the subchondral collapse and cartilage wear mechanism.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Severe joint dislocation tears the capsular and periarticular arterial supplies (e.g., circumflex vessels in the hip or shoulder). This produces subchondral avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) in the bone underlying the articular cartilage. Dead subchondral bone undergoes microfractures and mechanical collapse under weight-bearing stresses, leading to incongruity, shear stresses across the articular surface, and irreversible cartilage wear (secondary post-traumatic osteoarthritis).

questions.educationalObjective: Trace the sequence from capsular devascularization to subchondral osteonecrosis and cartilage degeneration.

questions.question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the ER with his left upper limb dangling flaccidly at his side. He refuses to move it. There were no direct witnesses, but the child cries and points to his older sister. On examination, the elbow is tender and swollen, with no other lesions. Clinical approach includes all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: Differential diagnosis includes soft tissue hematoma, subluxation of the bone in the elbow area, and fracture in the elbow area
options.B: X-ray will confirm or exclude some differential diagnoses
options.D: You ask the boy and his sister what happened
options.E: If it was a subluxation, it needs surgery to prevent fibrosis of the bone in its abnormal site

questions.explanation:
Subluxation of the radial head (nursemaid's elbow) is a closed, non-operative condition managed entirely by a simple, swift manual reduction maneuver (hyperpronation or supination-flexion) at the bedside in the clinic or ER. It NEVER requires open surgery, operative intervention, or prolonged immobilization.

High-yield: Nursemaid's elbow requires NO surgical repair. Spontaneous full recovery occurs after gentle closed manipulation.

Exam trap: Do not operate on simple radial head subluxations. However, if swelling and ecchymosis are present, obtain X-rays to rule out a fracture first, as nursemaid's elbow typically has NO swelling or bruising.

optionExplanations.A: Differential must include supracondylar fracture, lateral condyle fracture, nursemaid's elbow, and soft tissue contusion.
optionExplanations.B: Radiographs rule out bony fractures and posterior fat pad displacement.
optionExplanations.C: Standard orthopedic physical exam algorithm: Look (inspection), Feel (palpation), Move (range of motion).
optionExplanations.D: History taking from the child and witnesses is essential to understand potential mechanisms and screen for child abuse.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Subluxation of the radial head (nursemaid's elbow) is a closed, non-operative condition managed entirely by a simple, swift manual reduction maneuver (hyperpronation or supination-flexion) at the bedside in the clinic or ER. It NEVER requires open surgery, operative intervention, or prolonged immobilization.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that radial head subluxation is managed with bedside closed reduction, not surgery.

questions.question: In the human vertebral column (depicted in the anatomical diagram), you can find all of the following structural joint types EXCEPT:
questions.explanation:
Saddle (sellar) joints feature reciprocal concavo-convex articular surfaces (classic examples: first carpometacarpal joint of the thumb and sternoclavicular joint). There are NO saddle joints anywhere within the human vertebral column.

High-yield: Spinal Column Articulations: Symphyses (intervertebral discs), Synovial plane joints (facets C2-S1), Synovial pivot joint (median atlantoaxial C1-C2), Fibrous syndesmoses (spinal ligaments).

Exam trap: Do not confuse the uncovertable (Luschka) joints of the cervical spine with saddle joints; they are uncovertebral pseudo-joints/plane joints.

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Anatomical illustration of the complete human vertebral column with skull, showing cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral segments.

optionExplanations.A: Facet (zygapophyseal) joints are synovial plane gliding joints.
optionExplanations.B: Syndemoses (interspinous, supraspinous, and ligamentum flavum attachments) represent fibrous articulations.
optionExplanations.C: The median atlantoaxial (C1-C2) articulation is a classic synovial pivot (trochoid) joint.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Saddle (sellar) joints feature reciprocal concavo-convex articular surfaces (classic examples: first carpometacarpal joint of the thumb and sternoclavicular joint). There are NO saddle joints anywhere within the human vertebral column.
optionExplanations.E: Intervertebral discs are secondary cartilaginous joints (symphyses).

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate the joint classifications present in the vertebral column from peripheral joints.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy fell on an outstretched hand and complains of acute elbow pain, marked swelling, and limitation of elbow motion. An elbow radiograph report initially states 'no obvious fracture.' Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the radiologic evaluation of this case?

options.A: If the anterior humeral line passes anterior to the capitulum on the lateral elbow view, it would indicate a displaced supracondylar elbow fracture
options.B: Patient should be treated with crepe bandage and analgesia only
options.C: Radial neck fractures are the most common elbow injury
options.D: Reassurance of the family that there is no fracture based on the radiograph report

questions.explanation:
On a true lateral radiograph of a pediatric elbow, the Anterior Humeral Line (AHL) drawn along the anterior cortex of the humerus must intersect the middle third of the ossified capitellum. In extension-type supracondylar humerus fractures (the most common pediatric elbow fracture, ~60%), posterior displacement or angulation of the distal fragment causes the AHL to pass entirely ANTERIOR to the capitellum. Also, presence of a posterior fat pad sign ('sail sign') signifies an occult joint effusion/fracture.

High-yield: Pediatric Elbow Lines: (1) Anterior Humeral Line: intersects middle third of capitellum. (2) Radiocapitellar Line: straight line through radial neck bisects capitellum in ALL views.

Exam trap: A posterior fat pad on lateral elbow X-ray is ALWAYS pathological (indicates intraarticular hematoma/fracture). An anterior fat pad can be normal if thin, but a raised/displaced anterior fat pad ('sail sign') also indicates effusion.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. On a true lateral radiograph of a pediatric elbow, the Anterior Humeral Line (AHL) drawn along the anterior cortex of the humerus must intersect the middle third of the ossified capitellum. In extension-type supracondylar humerus fractures (the most common pediatric elbow fracture, ~60%), posterior displacement or angulation of the distal fragment causes the AHL to pass entirely ANTERIOR to the capitellum. Also, presence of a posterior fat pad sign ('sail sign') signifies an occult joint effusion/fracture.
optionExplanations.B: Treating a potentially unstable, neurovascularly vulnerable supracondylar fracture with a simple bandage leads to compartment syndrome, malunion (cubitus varus), and ischemic contracture.
optionExplanations.C: Supracondylar fractures of the distal humerus are by far the most common elbow fracture in children (55-65%), whereas radial neck fractures account for only 5-10%.
optionExplanations.D: Never discharge a symptomatic, swollen pediatric elbow on a preliminary negative report without checking the AHL, radiocapitellar line, and fat pads.
optionExplanations.E: Option A is correct, so 'none of the above' is wrong.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply the anterior humeral line on lateral elbow radiographs to diagnose pediatric supracondylar fractures.

questions.question: According to the radiographic image of a pediatric femoral fracture, which of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Rotational alignment and torsional displacement can be recognized on radiographs by comparing cortical diameters, profile discrepancies between the proximal and distal fragments, and the relationship between the femoral neck and distal condyles, although clinical examination provides definitive rotational confirmation.

High-yield: In pediatric femur fractures, remodeling can correct angulation and shortening over time, but rotational malalignment NEVER remodels spontaneously.

Exam trap: Never accept internal or external rotational malalignment in pediatric fractures under the assumption that remodeling will correct it.

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Pediatric femur radiograph demonstrating an oblique/spiral mid-diaphyseal fracture with displacement and rotational deformity.

[Review note] Key C ('easily shown rotational') conflicts with the bank's own teaching (ORTHO-009) that rotational alignment is judged clinically, not on radiographs. The question depends on an image that is not available. Source key retained.

optionExplanations.A: Comminuted or segmental patterns may contain secondary cortical fragments.
optionExplanations.B: Anatomical landmarks (femoral head, trochanters, condyles) and radiographic markers identify laterality.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Rotational alignment and torsional displacement can be recognized on radiographs by comparing cortical diameters, profile discrepancies between the proximal and distal fragments, and the relationship between the femoral neck and distal condyles, although clinical examination provides definitive rotational confirmation.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that rotational deformity in pediatric long-bone fractures requires anatomical correction because it does not remodel.

questions.question: What is the Salter-Harris classification of the distal tibial physeal fracture shown in the radiograph (demonstrating a fracture line extending across the metaphysis, through the physis, and exiting through the epiphysis into the articular joint)?
questions.explanation:
A Salter-Harris Type IV fracture extends through all three zones: Metaphysis, Physis (growth plate), and Epiphysis into the joint space (mnemonic: 'Through Everything'). Because it crosses the germinal layer of the physis and articular surface, it carries a high risk of physeal arrest, osseous bridging, and angular limb deformity, demanding anatomical open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF).

High-yield: SALTR Mnemonic: Type I = Straight across, Type II = Above (metaphysis), Type III = Lower (epiphysis), Type IV = Through/Two (metaphysis + epiphysis), Type V = Rammed (crush).

Exam trap: Types III and IV are intra-articular and disrupt the physis; they require exact anatomical reduction (<2 mm step-off) to prevent arthritis and growth arrest.

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Radiograph of the distal tibia and ankle showing a vertical fracture traversing from metaphysis across the growth plate into the epiphysis.

optionExplanations.A: Type I: Slipped (isolated physeal separation).
optionExplanations.B: Type II: Above (physis + metaphysis, Thurston-Holland fragment; most common type ~75%).
optionExplanations.C: Type III: Lower (physis + epiphysis into the joint, e.g., Tillaux fracture).
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A Salter-Harris Type IV fracture extends through all three zones: Metaphysis, Physis (growth plate), and Epiphysis into the joint space (mnemonic: 'Through Everything'). Because it crosses the germinal layer of the physis and articular surface, it carries a high risk of physeal arrest, osseous bridging, and angular limb deformity, demanding anatomical open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF).
optionExplanations.E: Type V: Rammed/Crush (axial compression crush injury to the physis).

questions.educationalObjective: Classify pediatric growth plate fractures using the Salter-Harris system, identifying Type IV as transphyseal.

questions.question: In the lateral elbow radiograph demonstrating a displaced extension-type supracondylar fracture of the humerus with posterolateral displacement of the distal fragment, which neural structure is at greatest risk of stretch or entrapment?
questions.explanation:
In extension-type supracondylar humeral fractures (especially with posterolateral displacement of the distal fragment), the proximal metaphyseal bone spike displaces anteriorly and medially, placing traction on the median nerve—specifically its deep motor branch, the Anterior Interosseous Nerve (AIN). AIN neuropraxia is the single most common nerve deficit, assessed by checking the patient's ability to make the 'OK sign' (flexion of the thumb IP joint by FPL and index DIP joint by FDP).

High-yield: Displaced supracondylar nerve injuries: Posterolateral displacement → Anterior Interosseous Nerve (AIN); Posteromedial displacement → Radial nerve; Flexion-type fracture → Ulnar nerve.

Exam trap: AIN is a pure motor nerve with NO sensory cutaneous distribution. Testing sensation on the hand will NOT detect an AIN palsy; you MUST test motor flexion of thumb IP and index DIP ('OK sign').

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Lateral elbow radiograph of a child demonstrating a displaced extension supracondylar fracture with sharp proximal humeral spike tenting anterior soft tissues.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. In extension-type supracondylar humeral fractures (especially with posterolateral displacement of the distal fragment), the proximal metaphyseal bone spike displaces anteriorly and medially, placing traction on the median nerve—specifically its deep motor branch, the Anterior Interosseous Nerve (AIN). AIN neuropraxia is the single most common nerve deficit, assessed by checking the patient's ability to make the 'OK sign' (flexion of the thumb IP joint by FPL and index DIP joint by FDP).
optionExplanations.B: PIN is a branch of the radial nerve injured in radial neck fractures or Monteggia fractures.
optionExplanations.C: Brachial artery (not radial artery) courses in the antecubital fossa alongside the median nerve and is at risk of entrapment.
optionExplanations.D: Veins are low-pressure structures not primarily assessed as definitive diagnostic markers.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the anterior interosseous nerve as the most vulnerable neural structure in extension supracondylar humerus fractures.

questions.question: Regarding the clinical photograph showing lower limb skin traction (Buck's traction) applied to a patient with an acute hip fracture, which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.D: Used temporary (1-2 days) for immobilization and alignment

questions.explanation:
Buck's skin traction is a non-invasive, temporary measure applied to the lower limb (typically using 5-7 lbs / 2-3 kg of weight) to provide provisional splinting, comfort, and reduction of painful muscle spasm while awaiting definitive surgical fixation (usually within 24-48 hours). It cannot maintain definitive skeletal reduction and should not be used long term.

High-yield: Maximum weight for skin traction is ~5-7 lbs (3 kg) to prevent skin sloughing, blistering, and peroneal nerve palsy. Skeletal traction (via tibial pin) is required for heavier loads (15-25 lbs).

Exam trap: Avoid excessive external rotation in Buck's traction as the fibular head can compress the common peroneal nerve against the mattress, causing foot drop.

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Clinical photo showing Buck's skin traction applied to the lower limb with adhesive foam wraps, cords, and pulley weight suspension.

optionExplanations.A: Skin traction is contraindicated over open wounds, severe abrasions, or fragile skin.
optionExplanations.B: Bryant's traction or Russell's traction is tailored for young pediatric femoral fractures; Buck's is predominantly adult/geriatric.
optionExplanations.C: Contact dermatitis can occur but is an uncommon adverse effect, not the primary defining operational feature.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Buck's skin traction is a non-invasive, temporary measure applied to the lower limb (typically using 5-7 lbs / 2-3 kg of weight) to provide provisional splinting, comfort, and reduction of painful muscle spasm while awaiting definitive surgical fixation (usually within 24-48 hours). It cannot maintain definitive skeletal reduction and should not be used long term.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize skin traction as a temporary, short-term measure (1-2 days) for comfort and alignment in hip fractures.

questions.question: Which of the following descriptions accurately characterizes the fracture displacement and deformity shown on the AP and lateral radiographs?

options.A: Shortening with posterior and medial apex angulation

questions.explanation:
Orthopedic fracture nomenclature describes displacement and angulation based on: (1) Translation/shortening (overriding of fragments causing limb shortening), (2) Angulation, designated by either the direction the apex points ('apex medial and posterior') or the direction the distal fragment is tilted.

High-yield: Standard fracture reporting: Location (diaphyseal/metaphyseal), Configuration (transverse, oblique, spiral), Displacement (% translation, shortening in cm), and Angulation (apex direction).

Exam trap: Clarify whether angulation is described by 'apex direction' (apex medial) or 'distal fragment tilt' (valgus); apex medial corresponds to varus deformity.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Orthopedic fracture nomenclature describes displacement and angulation based on: (1) Translation/shortening (overriding of fragments causing limb shortening), (2) Angulation, designated by either the direction the apex points ('apex medial and posterior') or the direction the distal fragment is tilted.
optionExplanations.B: Fail to account for both shortening and the true biplanar apex angulation depicted.
optionExplanations.C: Fail to account for both shortening and the true biplanar apex angulation depicted.
optionExplanations.D: Fail to account for both shortening and the true biplanar apex angulation depicted.

questions.question: Regarding the clinical photographs of hand motor postures following upper extremity trauma, which of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.A: Both A and B are radial nerve injury
options.B: B is due to posterior interosseous nerve injury
options.C: A is a claw hand deformity
options.D: A is due to anterior interosseous nerve injury

questions.explanation:
Image A demonstrates an inability to flex the interphalangeal joint of the thumb and the distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger when attempting to make a fist or pinch, characteristic of an Anterior Interosseous Nerve (AIN) lesion (paralyzing the flexor pollicis longus and lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus).

Exam trap: Distinguish AIN palsy (pure motor, no sensory deficit) from carpal tunnel syndrome (sensory loss in thumb/index/middle finger + thenar weakness).

optionExplanations.B: PIN injury causes finger and thumb extension loss without loss of wrist extension (ECRL is innervated by the main radial nerve before bifurcation).
optionExplanations.C: Claw hand deformity is caused by ulnar nerve injury (hyperextension of MCP and flexion of IP joints of 4th and 5th digits).

questions.question: A 78-year-old patient sustains an unstable intertrochanteric fracture of the proximal femur shown on the radiograph. What is the optimal surgical fixation method?

options.C: Minimal invasive in PFN (Proximal Femoral Nail / Intramedullary nail)

questions.explanation:
For unstable intertrochanteric femur fractures (especially those with reverse obliquity, loss of the posteromedial buttress, or subtrochanteric extension), cephalomedullary nailing (Proximal Femoral Nail [PFN] / Intramedullary Hip Screw) inserted via a minimally invasive percutaneous technique is the gold standard. Biomechanically, an intramedullary device has a shorter lever arm and superior load-sharing properties compared to extramedullary side-plates (DHS).

High-yield: Stable intertrochanteric fractures can be managed with DHS or Cephalomedullary nails; UNSTABLE intertrochanteric fractures mandate Cephalomedullary (intramedullary) nailing.

Exam trap: Tip-Apex Distance (TAD) <25 mm is required to prevent superior cut-out of the femoral neck lag screw.

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Radiograph demonstrating an unstable, comminuted intertrochanteric femoral fracture with subtrochanteric extension and lesser trochanter displacement.

optionExplanations.A: Extramedullary dynamic hip screws (DHS) have high failure and cut-out rates in unstable reverse-oblique patterns.
optionExplanations.B: 'Extramedullary nail' is a contradictory term; nails are intramedullary.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. For unstable intertrochanteric femur fractures (especially those with reverse obliquity, loss of the posteromedial buttress, or subtrochanteric extension), cephalomedullary nailing (Proximal Femoral Nail [PFN] / Intramedullary Hip Screw) inserted via a minimally invasive percutaneous technique is the gold standard. Biomechanically, an intramedullary device has a shorter lever arm and superior load-sharing properties compared to extramedullary side-plates (DHS).
optionExplanations.D: External fixation is reserved only for contaminated blast wounds or extreme damage control.

questions.question: A child presents after a fall on an outstretched hand. Forearm radiographs demonstrate cortical breach and angulation of the tension cortex of both radius and ulna, while the opposite cortices remain intact and bent. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.question: In the clinical examination of the patient shown below with a severe distal leg injury and open fracture, which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.B: We can see internal rotation of the distal leg and foot with plantar flexion of the ankle

options.D: Dressing should be done by the resident every time a doctor wants to see the wound to evaluate it
options.E: If the superficial peroneal nerve is affected, then this is the cause of foot drop

Inspection of the injured extremity demonstrates gross limb deformity consisting of internal rotation of the foot/distal segment combined with plantar flexion (equinus) at the ankle joint.

questions.question: A spiral fracture of a long bone is caused by which of the following physical mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Torsional (twisting) loading induces shear and tensile stresses acting obliquely at 45° to the bone's long axis, producing a characteristic spiral fracture that winds around the shaft.

High-yield: Twisting force on a planted foot = Spiral fracture of the tibia ('boot-top' ski injury) or spiral fracture of the humerus in arm wrestling.

optionExplanations.C: Direct blunt impact causes transverse or comminuted fractures.

questions.question: A 32-year-old male was involved in an MVA sustaining an open tibial fracture with active arterial bleeding. The patient is fully vaccinated according to childhood immunization schedules and received a tetanus toxoid booster 3 years ago. questions.question: A 67-year-old lady stumbled over a pavement and sustained severe ankle pain and swelling. X-rays and CT scans demonstrate a comminuted, intra-articular fracture of the distal tibial plafond with articular impaction and articular step-off (Pilon fracture). options.A: If there is a skin problem, the priority is the bad fracture, not the bad skin condition
options.C: There is comminution, but there is no step-off
options.D: The talus is broken as well as the distal tibia
options.E: The risk of post-traumatic arthritis is high

questions.explanation:
Pilon (tibial plafond) fractures involve high-energy axial impaction of the talus into the distal articular surface of the tibia, producing severe chondral damage, comminution, and articular step-off. Even with anatomical surgical reconstruction, the incidence of post-traumatic ankle osteoarthritis is exceedingly high (up to 50-70%).

Exam trap: Never perform immediate open reduction and internal fixation through swollen, blistered skin in a pilon fracture; wait for the soft tissues to settle.

optionExplanations.B: Pilon fractures are by definition intra-articular fractures of the weight-bearing tibial plafond.
optionExplanations.C: CT clearly demonstrates articular impaction and significant step-off.

questions.question: Claw hand deformity can be a clinical complication resulting from nerve injury in which of the following fracture presentations?

options.D: Supracondylar humeral fracture of flexion type in pediatric patients

questions.question: All of the following statements are true regarding a pediatric lateral condyle fracture of the distal humerus EXCEPT:

Because lateral condyle fractures cross the joint surface and are destabilized by extensor muscle pull, treatment of displaced fractures requires surgical pinning (CRPP or ORIF). Standard long-arm cast immobilization alone is insufficient and leads to nonunion.

High-yield: Lateral condyle fractures represent the second most common pediatric elbow fracture and have the highest rate of nonunion if managed inadequately.

questions.question: Regarding joint dislocations, all of the following statements are true EXCEPT:

options.A: Shoulder dislocation is the most common in adults
options.B: Dislocation could occur in any synovial joint

options.D: Shoulder dislocation occurs in a bimodal age group
options.E: Reduction of hip dislocation should occur by conscious sedation in the ER

questions.explanation:
While emergency reduction of a dislocated hip is critical (<6 hours), the hip is surrounded by the largest and most powerful muscular envelope in the body (glutei, iliopsoas, rotators). Attempting reduction under light 'conscious sedation' frequently fails due to intense muscle spasm and risks iatrogenic femoral neck fracture. Deep procedural sedation or general anesthesia with profound neuromuscular relaxation in the operating room (or well-equipped resuscitation bay) is required for safe, atraumatic closed reduction (Allis or Captain Morgan technique).

High-yield: Traumatic hip dislocation requires urgent reduction (<6 hours) with adequate muscle relaxation to prevent femoral head osteonecrosis.

Exam trap: Never forcefully lever a dislocated hip against unyielding muscular resistance; this can fracture the femoral neck, converting a dislocated native hip into an irreparable catastrophe.

optionExplanations.C: Violent internal rotator tetany in electrocution causes posterior shoulder dislocation.
optionExplanations.D: Shoulder dislocations demonstrate a bimodal distribution: young athletic males (high-energy) and elderly females (low-energy falls).

questions.question: A 23-year-old factory worker sustained a severe machinery crush injury with his left forearm entrapped between cylindrical rollers. He presents with severe pain, tense swelling, and paresthesias. Photographs show the limb before and after dual volar and dorsal fasciotomies. Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding this condition?

options.A: Both the anatomical spaces of flexor and extensor tendons are affected
options.B: The diagnosis condition occurs only after trauma
options.C: Treatment should be done within 3 days
options.D: Median nerve is spared in this condition

questions.explanation:
Severe crush injuries with untreated compartment syndrome lead to massive muscle necrosis (rhabdomyolysis). The systemic release of massive potassium (causing fatal cardiac arrhythmias), myoglobin (causing acute tubular necrosis and renal failure), and thromboplastin (causing disseminated intravascular coagulation [DIC]) makes severe crush compartment syndrome a LIFE-THREATENING systemic disease (Crush Syndrome / Bywaters syndrome).

High-yield: Forearm compartments: Volar (flexor), Dorsal (extensor), and Mobile Wad. Volar fasciotomy requires release of the lacertus fibrosus, superficial/deep flexors, and carpal tunnel.

Exam trap: Late fasciotomy (>36-48 hours after muscle death) carries high risk of uncontrollable infection and sepsis; late cases require medical support or amputation.

questions.question: A 32-year-old male was involved in a motor vehicle accident with an open wound and active bleeding from the posterior tibial artery. questions.question: An 8-year-old girl was admitted with a severely displaced supracondylar fracture of the left humerus. What is the EARLIEST and most sensitive clinical sign alerting the physician to developing acute compartment syndrome of the forearm?

options.A: Severe pain upon passive stretching of her flexors

questions.explanation:
The earliest, most reliable, and most sensitive clinical hallmark of acute compartment syndrome in a conscious patient is severe, unremitting pain that is disproportionate to the underlying injury and excruciating pain elicited by passive stretching of the muscles within the affected compartment (passive finger extension for the volar forearm). In children, increased analgesia requirement ('the 3 A's': Anxiety, Agitation, and Analgesia requirement) is equally crucial.

High-yield: Pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch = Earliest signs of Compartment Syndrome. Pulselessness and paralysis = Late, irreversible signs.

Exam trap: Never rule out compartment syndrome because distal pulses are intact and capillary refill is brisk; perfusion pressure can be completely adequate to generate a pulse while tissue microcirculation is dead.

questions.question: An electrician presents with pain along the radial aspect of the wrist near the base of the thumb that has gradually worsened over several weeks with repetitive gripping. There is no history of trauma. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in conservative management?

options.A: Finkelstein's test is not used for diagnosis
options.B: Local NSAID therapy alone is sufficient
options.D: Surgery is prioritized in this case

De Quervain's tenosynovitis involves stenosing tenosynovitis of the first dorsal extensor compartment (abductor pollicis longus [APL] and extensor pollicis brevis [EPB]). For moderate-to-severe or persistent symptoms, the most effective conservative management is corticosteroid infiltration into the tendon sheath combined with thumb spica splint immobilization.

High-yield: First dorsal compartment contents: APL and EPB ('Apple with Peanut Butter'). Corticosteroid injection achieves cure in >80% of patients.

Exam trap: Beware of anatomical variants during surgical release: multiple sub-compartments or slip tendons (especially of APL) can lead to incomplete release and persistent pain.

optionExplanations.C: Correct. questions.question: A lateral foot radiograph demonstrates a prominent plantar calcaneal spur in a patient with severe chronic inferior heel pain. Which of the following biomechanical abnormalities is the most probable predisposing cause for this condition?

options.B: Short Achilles tendon (Equinus contracture / Gastrocnemius tightness)

questions.explanation:
A tight, shortened Achilles tendon (gastrocnemius-soleus tightness / equinus contracture) limits ankle dorsiflexion during the stance phase of gait. To compensate, the foot undergoes excessive pronation, which markedly increases tensile load and repetitive micro-traction across the plantar fascia at its origin on the calcaneal tuberosity, leading to plantar fasciitis and secondary traction spur formation.

High-yield: The Silfverskiöld test differentiates isolated gastrocnemius tightness from Achilles tendon (gastroc-soleus) contracture by checking dorsiflexion with the knee flexed vs. extended.

Exam trap: The calcaneal spur itself is NOT the cause of pain; it is a harmless traction osteophyte. Pain originates from microtears and chronic fasciosis of the plantar fascia.

To compensate, the foot undergoes excessive pronation, which markedly increases tensile load and repetitive micro-traction across the plantar fascia at its origin on the calcaneal tuberosity, leading to plantar fasciitis and secondary traction spur formation.

questions.question: Which of the following scenarios represents the accepted clinical indication for surgical intervention (partial plantar fasciotomy) in plantar fasciitis?

options.B: In the acute phase, to relieve pain
options.C: In cases of chronic years of plantar fasciitis (refractory to conservative therapy for >6-12 months)

Exam trap: Never rush to surgery in plantar fasciitis; conservative therapy requires months of patient compliance to succeed.

Over 90-95% of patients with plantar fasciitis recover completely with conservative management (Achilles/plantar fascia stretching, night splints, orthotics, NSAIDs, physical therapy). questions.question: A 70-year-old female fell on her outstretched wrist one week ago. She presents with persistent severe wrist pain, marked paresthesias in the thumb and index finger, and developing thenar muscle weakness/atrophy. Wrist radiographs demonstrate volar displacement of the lunate into the carpal tunnel. What is the definitive management?

Volar lunate dislocation directly compresses the median nerve against the transverse carpal ligament, producing acute carpal tunnel syndrome. Progressive thenar muscle weakness and sensory loss demand emergent open/closed reduction of the displaced lunate accompanied by surgical division (release) of the transverse carpal ligament to decompress the median nerve.

Exam trap: Acute median nerve compression from lunate dislocation is a surgical emergency; delayed reduction causes permanent thenar paralysis and sensory loss.

optionExplanations.B: Correct. Volar lunate dislocation directly compresses the median nerve against the transverse carpal ligament, producing acute carpal tunnel syndrome. Progressive thenar muscle weakness and sensory loss demand emergent open/closed reduction of the displaced lunate accompanied by surgical division (release) of the transverse carpal ligament to decompress the median nerve.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with severe right shoulder pain that began abruptly 2 days ago and has progressively worsened. She denies trauma. options.B: Can be treated by Infiltration therapy with follow up
options.C: The deposition phase is more painful and clinically relevant

questions.explanation:
This patient has acute Calcific Tendinitis of the rotator cuff (calcium hydroxyapatite crystal deposition, most commonly in the supraspinatus tendon). First-line management is conservative: subacromial corticosteroid infiltration, NSAIDs, and physical therapy, with needle barbotage/lavage reserved for refractory cases.

Exam trap: The resorptive phase produces agonizing pain mimicking acute septic arthritis; fever and high ESR/CRP are absent, and radiographs confirm calcium resorption.

First-line management is conservative: subacromial corticosteroid infiltration, NSAIDs, and physical therapy, with needle barbotage/lavage reserved for refractory cases.

questions.question: The rotator cuff consists of four dynamic glenohumeral stabilizing muscles. Which of the following muscles is NOT a component of the rotator cuff?
questions.explanation:

questions.question: Finkelstein's provocative test is used clinically for the definitive diagnosis of which condition?
questions.explanation:

Severe sharp pain along the radial styloid process confirms stenosing tenosynovitis of the first extensor compartment (De Quervain's disease).

High-yield: De Quervain's tenosynovitis classically affects postpartum women lifting newborns ('baby wrist') and racquet sports players.

questions.question: What is the historical gold standard and mainstay definitive surgical treatment for advanced, disabling Dupuytren's contracture?

High-yield: Indications for surgery in Dupuytren's: MCP joint contracture >30° or ANY PIP joint contracture (even 5-10°), or a positive 'Hueston tabletop test' (inability to place palm flat on table).

Exam trap: Never excise palmar skin indiscriminately; Bruner zig-zag incisions or open palm technique (McCash) are employed to prevent contracture recurrence.

questions.question: A 60-year-old male presents with bilateral palmar nodular thickening and progressive flexion contractures of the ring and small fingers (Dupuytren's contracture). Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding this disease?

These cells generate contractile forces that form nodules and shorten into thick pretendinous cords, pulling the fingers into fixed flexion contractures.

High-yield: Risk factors for Dupuytren's: Northern European ancestry, male sex (>50 years), smoking, alcohol use, diabetes mellitus, chronic antiepileptic therapy, and liver cirrhosis.

Exam trap: Dupuytren's disease involves the palmar fascia and aponeurosis, NOT the flexor tendons; the flexor tendons glide normally beneath the diseased fascia.

optionExplanations.D: NSAIDs provide zero therapeutic benefit against fibrogenesis.

questions.question: 'Tennis elbow' is the common clinical designation for which condition?
questions.explanation:
Tennis elbow is Lateral Epicondylitis (or lateral epicondylalgia/tendinosis), an overuse tendinopathy primarily affecting the common extensor tendon origin at the lateral epicondyle of the humerus, specifically involving the Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis (ECRB) origin.

High-yield: Key muscle in Lateral Epicondylitis: Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis (ECRB). Pain is provoked by resisted wrist extension and resisted middle finger extension (Maudsley's test).

questions.question: Comprehensive non-operative and surgical treatment options for refractory tennis elbow (lateral epicondylitis) include which of the following?

Management of lateral epicondylitis encompasses a broad spectrum: conservative measures include counterforce forearm straps/braces (which dissipate tensile forces distal to the epicondyle), physiotherapy with eccentric strengthening, and corticosteroid/PRP injections. questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding Dupuytren's contracture is FALSE?

questions.question: A 60-year-old male patient presents with progressive, severe shoulder stiffness and deep aching pain that developed after 6 weeks of prolonged sling immobilization following a distal radius fracture. Active and passive glenohumeral ranges of motion are severely and equally restricted in all planes (especially external rotation). What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is a fibroproliferative contracture of the glenohumeral capsule and coracohumeral ligament resulting in obliterative fibrosis of the axillary recess. It frequently develops secondary to prolonged immobilization (post-fracture, post-stroke, postsurgery) or in patients with diabetes mellitus and thyroid disease. The hallmark physical finding is severe, EQUAL reduction in BOTH active AND passive range of motion, with external rotation being the most dramatically restricted.

High-yield: Key Clinical Differentiator: Rotator Cuff Tear = Restricted Active motion, NORMAL Passive motion. Adhesive Capsulitis = Severely RESTRICTED Active AND Passive motion (especially external rotation).

Exam trap: Diabetes mellitus is the strongest systemic risk factor for adhesive capsulitis; diabetic patients have higher rates of bilateral involvement and resistance to conservative therapy.

Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) is a fibroproliferative contracture of the glenohumeral capsule and coracohumeral ligament resulting in obliterative fibrosis of the axillary recess. It frequently develops secondary to prolonged immobilization (post-fracture, post-stroke, postsurgery) or in patients with diabetes mellitus and thyroid disease. questions.question: In pediatric septic arthritis of the hip, which characteristic limb posture does the patient spontaneously adopt to minimize intracapsular pressure and relieve agonizing joint pain?

options.A: hip flexion, abduction and externally rotation

In septic arthritis of the hip, joint effusion generates extreme intracapsular hydrostatic pressure. The position of maximal capsular volume and compliance is FLEXION, ABDUCTION, and EXTERNAL ROTATION ('FABER' posture). Patients hold the limb rigidly in this position; any attempt at passive extension or internal rotation spikes intracapsular pressure, triggering intense pain and muscle guarding.

High-yield: Positions of Maximum Capsular Volume: Hip = Flexion, Abduction, External rotation; Knee = 30° Flexion; Elbow = 70-80° Flexion.

Exam trap: Never forcefully extend or internally rotate an infant's hip if septic arthritis is suspected; doing so risks tamponading retinacular vessels and inducing ischemic femoral head necrosis.

questions.question: A patient presents with acute monoarticular joint pain, severe erythema, warmth, and joint swelling without history of trauma or known drug allergies. Serum inflammatory markers reveal marked leukocytosis and elevated CRP. What is the most appropriate initial empiric antistaphylococcal antibiotic?
questions.explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus is the causative pathogen in >70-80% of acute septic arthritis and osteomyelitis cases. In non-allergic patients in regions with methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA), penicillinase-resistant penicillins (Oxacillin, Nafcillin, Flucloxacillin) are the definitive first-line bactericidal agents targeting cell wall synthesis.

High-yield: Empiric coverage for Septic Arthritis: Healthy adult/child = Antistaphylococcal penicillin (Oxacillin/Nafcillin) or Cefazolin (add Vancomycin if MRSA risk); Sexually active young adult = Ceftriaxone (covers N. gonorrhoeae).

Exam trap: Always obtain synovial fluid aspirate for Gram stain and culture BEFORE administering the first dose of antibiotics.

In non-allergic patients in regions with methicillin-susceptible S. aureus (MSSA), penicillinase-resistant penicillins (Oxacillin, Nafcillin, Flucloxacillin) are the definitive first-line bactericidal agents targeting cell wall synthesis.

questions.question: For the comprehensive antibiotic management of uncomplicated pediatric septic arthritis, what is the standard recommended duration of antimicrobial therapy?

options.A: 2 weeks of IV antibiotics followed by 2 weeks of oral therapy (Total 3-4 weeks)
options.C: Oral antibiotics should never be used because they do not adequately penetrate the joint
options.D: it has the same period of osteomyelitis

Standard pediatric orthopedic protocols for uncomplicated septic arthritis recommend a total duration of 3 to 4 weeks of antimicrobial therapy. This traditionally consists of initial parenteral (IV) antibiotics for 1 to 2 weeks until clinical improvement (afebrile, resolving effusion, downtrending CRP by >50%), followed by transition to high-dose targeted oral therapy for an additional 2 to 3 weeks.

High-yield: Criteria for Oral Transition: Patient is afebrile for >24-48 hours, tolerating oral intake, marked reduction in joint pain/effusion, and CRP has decreased by at least 50%.

Exam trap: Do not transition to oral antibiotics if CRP remains elevated or if the child is still febrile.

This traditionally consists of initial parenteral (IV) antibiotics for 1 to 2 weeks until clinical improvement (afebrile, resolving effusion, downtrending CRP by >50%), followed by transition to high-dose targeted oral therapy for an additional 2 to 3 weeks.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the pathological entity termed a 'Sequestrum' in chronic osteomyelitis?

options.A: devitalized tissue due to vascular stripping (Necrotic bone separated from living bone)

questions.explanation:
A sequestrum is a segment of necrotic, devitalized bone that has become separated from living, vascularized osseous tissue during the process of osteomyelitis. It arises when rising subperiosteal and intramedullary pus strips the periosteum and thromboses nutrient haversian and periosteal blood vessels, causing ischemic necrosis.

High-yield: Pathological hallmarks of Chronic Osteomyelitis: Sequestrum (dead bone island), Involucrum (new periosteal bone sheath), and Cloaca (draining sinus tract opening).

Exam trap: Antibiotics cannot penetrate a sequestrum because it has no blood supply; cure requires surgical sequestrectomy.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A sequestrum is a segment of necrotic, devitalized bone that has become separated from living, vascularized osseous tissue during the process of osteomyelitis. It arises when rising subperiosteal and intramedullary pus strips the periosteum and thromboses nutrient haversian and periosteal blood vessels, causing ischemic necrosis.
optionExplanations.B: Reactive new bone formation surrounding the sequestrum is termed the INVOLUCRUM.
optionExplanations.C: While bacterial biofilms form on sequestra, the anatomical and pathological definition of a sequestrum is devitalized/necrotic bone.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial empiric antibiotic regimen for a Gustilo-Anderson Grade III open fracture?
questions.explanation:

The involucrum is living subperiosteal reactive new bone synthesized by the periosteum around the dead sequestrum in chronic osteomyelitis.
