Exam trap: The involucrum can be seen on plain X-rays as an irregular outer bony collar surrounding a radiolucent space containing dense sequestra.

optionExplanations.A: Defines the sequestrum.
optionExplanations.B: Defines a cloaca.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The involucrum is living subperiosteal reactive new bone synthesized by the periosteum around the dead sequestrum in chronic osteomyelitis.
optionExplanations.D: This describes the enhancing rim of an abscess or soft-tissue collection, not bone formed around a sequestrum.
optionExplanations.E: A thickened joint capsule is a sequela of joint inflammation or sepsis; it is not an involucrum.

questions.educationalObjective: Confirm the definition of an involucrum as reactive new bone enclosing a sequestrum.

questions.question: Which of the following clinical factors predispose an adult patient to the development of acute septic arthritis?
questions.explanation:
Adult septic arthritis occurs almost predominantly in patients with identifiable predisposing risk factors: systemic immunosuppression (steroids, chemotherapy, diabetes), prosthetic joint implants, damaged joints with pre-existing synovial pathology (Rheumatoid arthritis is the strongest risk factor due to vascular hyperplasia and defective phagocytosis), and invasive intra-articular procedures.

High-yield: Rheumatoid Arthritis is the #1 predisposing chronic joint disease for septic arthritis. Always suspect septic arthritis when a single joint flares disproportionately in an RA patient.

Exam trap: Never assume a single hot, swollen joint in an RA or gout patient is merely an underlying disease flare; arthrocentesis must be performed to rule out superimposed septic arthritis.

optionExplanations.A: All are major verified risk factors; therefore 'All of the above' is correct.
optionExplanations.B: All are major verified risk factors; therefore 'All of the above' is correct.
optionExplanations.C: All are major verified risk factors; therefore 'All of the above' is correct.
optionExplanations.D: All are major verified risk factors; therefore 'All of the above' is correct.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Adult septic arthritis occurs almost predominantly in patients with identifiable predisposing risk factors: systemic immunosuppression (steroids, chemotherapy, diabetes), prosthetic joint implants, damaged joints with pre-existing synovial pathology (Rheumatoid arthritis is the strongest risk factor due to vascular hyperplasia and defective phagocytosis), and invasive intra-articular procedures.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify key predisposing factors for adult septic arthritis, including rheumatoid arthritis and immunosuppression.

questions.question: The most common etiology/transmission route for acute osteomyelitis in children is:
questions.explanation:
Hematogenous seeding is the primary cause of acute osteomyelitis in children.

High-yield: Most common sites of hematogenous osteomyelitis in children: Distal femur, Proximal tibia, and Proximal humerus.

Exam trap: Initial radiographs are often normal for the first 10-14 days; do not delay treatment if clinical suspicion is high.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Hematogenous seeding is the primary cause of acute osteomyelitis in children.
optionExplanations.B: Direct inoculation occurs through open fractures or penetrating puncture wounds, which are less common overall in children.
optionExplanations.C: Predisposing host factors, but the primary route of transmission is hematogenous bacteremia.
optionExplanations.D: Predisposing host factors, but the primary route of transmission is hematogenous bacteremia.
optionExplanations.E: Predisposing host factors, but the primary route of transmission is hematogenous bacteremia.

questions.educationalObjective: Confirm hematogenous seeding as the primary route of infection in pediatric osteomyelitis.

questions.question: In which of the following pediatric patients with acute osteomyelitis of the tibia is surgical debridement and subperiosteal/intramedullary drainage the most appropriate immediate next step in management?

options.A: A 7-year-old girl with 3 days of pain, fever, and WBCs of 21,000 who presents to the ER
options.B: An 8-year-old lethargic girl with WBCs of 21,000 and CRP of 9 after 24 hours of gentamicin
options.C: An 8-year-old boy whose pain and fever had decreased after 24 hours of gentamicin
options.D: A 9-year-old girl with new onset of pain and fever
options.E: A 7-year-old lethargic boy with CRP of 20 that does not decline after a week of nafcillin and vancomycin

questions.explanation:
Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in children is initially managed medically with targeted IV antibiotics. Definitive indications for surgical intervention include: (1) Failure to improve clinically (persistent fever, pain, lethargy) or serologically (failure of CRP to decline) after 24-48 hours (and especially after 1 week) of appropriate IV antibiotics, (2) Presence of a drainable subperiosteal or intraosseous abscess on ultrasound or MRI, or (3) Cortical bone necrosis/sequestrum.

High-yield: Treatment failure in acute osteomyelitis: Persistent fever + non-declining CRP after 48-72 hours of IV antibiotics = Mandatory MRI and surgical debridement/decompression.

Exam trap: Do not operate on acute uncomplicated hematogenous osteomyelitis in children that is responding well to IV antibiotics.

optionExplanations.A: Initial presentations before attempting empiric IV antibiotic therapy; medical management is tried first unless a large subperiosteal abscess is identified.
optionExplanations.B: CRP of 9 represents a downtrend, and 24 hours is too early to declare medical failure if vitals are stabilizing.
optionExplanations.C: Clinical improvement (resolving fever and pain) indicates medical success; surgery is not required.
optionExplanations.D: Initial presentations before attempting empiric IV antibiotic therapy; medical management is tried first unless a large subperiosteal abscess is identified.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in children is initially managed medically with targeted IV antibiotics. Definitive indications for surgical intervention include: (1) Failure to improve clinically (persistent fever, pain, lethargy) or serologically (failure of CRP to decline) after 24-48 hours (and especially after 1 week) of appropriate IV antibiotics, (2) Presence of a drainable subperiosteal or intraosseous abscess on ultrasound or MRI, or (3) Cortical bone necrosis/sequestrum.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify clinical and laboratory non-response to IV antibiotics as an absolute indication for surgical debridement in osteomyelitis.

questions.question: The most common causative agent of septic arthritis in children across all demographics is:
questions.explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus is the leading bacterial cause of pediatric septic arthritis.

High-yield: Kocher Criteria for Septic Hip in Children: (1) Non-weight bearing on affected side, (2) ESR >40 mm/hr, (3) Fever >38.5°C, (4) WBC >12,000/mm³. 4/4 criteria = 99% probability of septic arthritis.

Exam trap: Differentiating septic arthritis from transient synovitis: Transient synovitis patients are mildly uncomfortable but usually bear some weight, have normal/mild inflammatory markers, and improve rapidly with rest.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Staphylococcus aureus is the leading bacterial cause of pediatric septic arthritis.
optionExplanations.B: Streptococcus pneumoniae incidence has fallen markedly following routine pneumococcal conjugate vaccination.
optionExplanations.C: H. influenzae type b was historically common in children <2 years, but is now rare due to the Hib vaccine.
optionExplanations.D: Kingella kingae is common in toddlers (6-36 months), but S. aureus is the most common overall across pediatric age groups.
optionExplanations.E: Brucella causes chronic osteoarticular infection in endemic areas associated with unpasteurized dairy.

questions.educationalObjective: Reiterate Staphylococcus aureus as the premier pathogen in pediatric septic arthritis.

questions.question: In chronic osteomyelitis, a sequestrum is precisely defined as:

options.C: Healthy bone adjacent to chronic osteomyelitis
options.D: Healthy bone adjacent to acute osteomyelitis
options.E: Necrotic bone providing a nidus for infection in chronic osteomyelitis

questions.explanation:
A sequestrum represents devitalized bone detached from healthy bone acting as a reservoir for bacterial biofilms.

High-yield: CT scan is the best imaging modality to identify sequestra and plan surgical sequestrectomy.

Exam trap: Antibiotics alone will never cure chronic osteomyelitis in the presence of a sequestrum; surgical removal is mandatory.

optionExplanations.A: Reactive new bone is the involucrum.
optionExplanations.B: Reactive new bone is the involucrum.
optionExplanations.C: Sequestrum is dead, necrotic, avascular bone—not healthy bone.
optionExplanations.D: Sequestrum is dead, necrotic, avascular bone—not healthy bone.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. A sequestrum represents devitalized bone detached from healthy bone acting as a reservoir for bacterial biofilms.

questions.educationalObjective: Confirm the pathological definition of a sequestrum.

questions.question: In the diagnostic investigation of acute or chronic osteomyelitis, which of the following modalities is NOT used?
questions.explanation:
Angiography is not used for diagnosing osteomyelitis.

High-yield: Bone biopsy via fluoroscopic or CT guidance (taking care not to traverse cellulitic skin) is the gold standard for bacteriological diagnosis.

Exam trap: Never rely on superficial skin or sinus tract swabs; they reflect colonizing flora, not the deep causative bone pathogen.

optionExplanations.A: MRI has >90% sensitivity/specificity; bone scan is useful when MRI is contraindicated.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Angiography is not used for diagnosing osteomyelitis.
optionExplanations.C: X-rays rule out other pathology, and US detects subperiosteal fluid collections in children.
optionExplanations.D: CRP and ESR assess systemic inflammation and monitor therapeutic response.
optionExplanations.E: Bone biopsy provides the definitive microbiological culture.

questions.educationalObjective: Confirm that angiography has no diagnostic role in osteomyelitis.

questions.question: In cases of periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) associated with total joint arthroplasty, which of the following statements is FALSE?

options.A: Presence of a foreign material can provide bacteria with an excellent opportunity for binding and colonization
options.B: Treatment of infected arthroplasties involves removal of the old implant, including all the cement mantle, aggressive irrigation and debridement
options.C: Radiographs can demonstrate subtle or even profound bone resorption surrounding implants suspected of being infected
options.D: Patients with cultures positive for bacteria should undergo reimplantation
options.E: A cement spacer impregnated with antibiotics is usually implanted at the time of initial debridement

questions.explanation:
In two-stage exchange arthroplasty (the gold standard for chronic PJI), the first stage consists of complete implant removal, aggressive debridement of infected soft tissue and bone, removal of all bone cement, and insertion of an articulating or static antibiotic-loaded polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) cement spacer. Reimplantation of a new definitive prosthesis is strictly performed ONLY AFTER complete eradication of the infection (confirmed by normalized inflammatory markers, clinical quiescence, and negative repeat joint aspirate cultures). Reimplanting a permanent prosthesis while cultures are still positive for active bacteria leads to catastrophic re-infection and is completely false.

High-yield: Two-Stage Exchange Arthroplasty Protocol: Stage 1: Explant hardware + debride + antibiotic cement spacer + 6 weeks of targeted IV/oral antibiotics. Stage 2: 4-6 week antibiotic-free holiday → Confirm sterile joint aspirate → Re-implant definitive revision prosthesis.

Exam trap: Never re-implant a definitive joint prosthesis if joint aspiration demonstrates persistent bacteria or elevated synovial alpha-defensin / leukocyte esterase.

optionExplanations.A: Prosthetic biomaterials allow glycocalyx biofilm formation by Staphylococcus epidermidis and S. aureus.
optionExplanations.B: Complete debridement and cement extraction are vital because biofilm adheres to cement and metal.
optionExplanations.C: Rapid, osteolytic peri-implant bone resorption, osteopenia, and lucency >2 mm at the bone-cement interface indicate infection or loosening.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. In two-stage exchange arthroplasty (the gold standard for chronic PJI), the first stage consists of complete implant removal, aggressive debridement of infected soft tissue and bone, removal of all bone cement, and insertion of an articulating or static antibiotic-loaded polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) cement spacer. Reimplantation of a new definitive prosthesis is strictly performed ONLY AFTER complete eradication of the infection (confirmed by normalized inflammatory markers, clinical quiescence, and negative repeat joint aspirate cultures). Reimplanting a permanent prosthesis while cultures are still positive for active bacteria leads to catastrophic re-infection and is completely false.
optionExplanations.E: High-dose antibiotic-impregnated cement spacers (vancomycin + tobramycin) elute high local antibiotic concentrations.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that definitive prosthetic reimplantation in PJI is contraindicated until active bacterial infection is completely eradicated.

questions.question: In knee osteoarthritis, plain radiographs demonstrate all of the following classic degenerative changes EXCEPT:
questions.explanation:
Sequestrum and involucrum are the signature pathological lesions of chronic osteomyelitis, not osteoarthritis.

High-yield: Knee OA classic progression: Cartilage loss → Asymmetrical joint space narrowing → Subchondral bone remodeling (sclerosis) → Marginal osteophytes → Fixed deformity (varus in medial OA, valgus in lateral OA).

Exam trap: Do not mistake osteophytes at the joint margin for avulsion fractures.

optionExplanations.A: Classic cardinal radiographic features of knee osteoarthritis.
optionExplanations.B: Classic cardinal radiographic features of knee osteoarthritis.
optionExplanations.C: Classic cardinal radiographic features of knee osteoarthritis.
optionExplanations.D: Classic cardinal radiographic features of knee osteoarthritis.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Sequestrum and involucrum are the signature pathological lesions of chronic osteomyelitis, not osteoarthritis.

questions.educationalObjective: Reiterate that sequestrum and involucrum are features of osteomyelitis, not osteoarthritis.

questions.question: Diagnostic investigation of aspirated joint synovial fluid in suspected acute septic arthritis routinely includes all of the following laboratory evaluations EXCEPT:
questions.explanation:
Standard diagnostic synovial fluid analysis (arthrocentesis) for suspected septic arthritis includes: (1) Gross visual appearance (clarity, color, viscosity), (2) Total white blood cell (WBC) count and percentage of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs), (3) Gram stain, (4) Microbiological cultures and susceptibilities, and (5) Polarized light microscopy to rule out crystal-induced arthropathies (gout/pseudogout). Synovial fluid 'antibody count' is non-standard, non-validated, and has no clinical utility in evaluating acute joint sepsis.

High-yield: Synovial Fluid Categories: Normal (<200 WBC, <25% PMN); Non-inflammatory (200-2,000 WBC, OA); Inflammatory (2,000-50,000 WBC, RA/gout); Septic (>50,000 WBC, >75% PMN).

Exam trap: Crystals and bacteria can coexist! Never assume a joint is non-infected just because crystals are identified on polarized microscopy; send for culture.

optionExplanations.A: Gram stain provides rapid preliminary identification in ~50-60% of cases.
optionExplanations.B: Aerobic and anaerobic cultures identify the pathogen and determine antibiotic sensitivities.
optionExplanations.C: Leukocyte count >50,000/mm³ with >75-90% neutrophils strongly supports septic arthritis.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Standard diagnostic synovial fluid analysis (arthrocentesis) for suspected septic arthritis includes: (1) Gross visual appearance (clarity, color, viscosity), (2) Total white blood cell (WBC) count and percentage of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs), (3) Gram stain, (4) Microbiological cultures and susceptibilities, and (5) Polarized light microscopy to rule out crystal-induced arthropathies (gout/pseudogout). Synovial fluid 'antibody count' is non-standard, non-validated, and has no clinical utility in evaluating acute joint sepsis.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall the essential components of synovial fluid analysis in suspected septic arthritis, excluding antibody testing.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following is an established secondary radiographic/MRI indicator of a complete anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture?

options.A: Buckled posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) on MRI
options.B: Firm endpoint in the anterior drawer test

questions.explanation:
When the anterior cruciate ligament completely ruptures, the tibia translates anteriorly relative to the femur. Because the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) is tethered between the posterior tibia and medial femoral condyle, this anterior tibial shift releases tension on the PCL, causing it to buckle with an acute curvature angle (<105°) on sagittal MRI (known as 'PCL buckling sign').

High-yield: Secondary MRI Signs of ACL Tear: PCL buckling, bone contusion kissing contusions on lateral femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau, anterior tibial translation >7 mm, uncovering of posterior horn of lateral meniscus, and Segond fracture.

Exam trap: Lachman test (at 20-30° flexion) is clinically much more sensitive (~85-90%) than the anterior drawer test (at 90° flexion, ~60-70%) for detecting acute ACL tears.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. When the anterior cruciate ligament completely ruptures, the tibia translates anteriorly relative to the femur. Because the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) is tethered between the posterior tibia and medial femoral condyle, this anterior tibial shift releases tension on the PCL, causing it to buckle with an acute curvature angle (<105°) on sagittal MRI (known as 'PCL buckling sign').
optionExplanations.B: A complete ACL tear yields a SOFT or absent endpoint on Lachman and anterior drawer tests.
optionExplanations.C: Classic bone contusion pattern in acute pivot-shift ACL injury is on the LATERAL femoral condyle and posterolateral tibial plateau (not posteromedial).
optionExplanations.D: Joint effusion/hemarthrosis is a non-specific finding common to many acute knee injuries; it is not an established secondary sign of complete ACL rupture (the key is PCL buckling).
optionExplanations.E: Normal ACL has a straight, taut anterior margin; in tears, it is wavy, retracted, or absent.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify PCL buckling on sagittal MRI as a secondary sign of complete ACL rupture.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the vascular anatomy and zones of the medial meniscus?

options.A: The pink zone is the outer 3 mm rim
options.B: The red zone is located near the femoral condyle
options.C: The white zone is avascular and located centrally
options.D: The red zone represents the inner two-thirds of the meniscus

questions.explanation:
Arnar vascular supply to the menisci arises from the medial and lateral genicular arteries through the perimeniscal capillary plexus. The meniscus is divided into three vascular zones: (1) Red-Red Zone (outer 10-25% / outer 1-3 mm, fully vascularized with high healing potential), (2) Red-White Zone (intermediate border, intermediate vascularity), and (3) White-White Zone (inner 60-70% / inner two-thirds, completely AVASCULAR, nourished solely by synovial fluid diffusion, with zero intrinsic healing potential).

High-yield: Surgical rule: Tears in the Red-Red zone are REPAIRED (arthroscopic suturing) to preserve joint function; tears in the White-White zone will not heal and are DEBRIDED (partial meniscectomy).

Exam trap: Do not attempt to suture an isolated complex tear in the avascular white-white zone; it will fail to heal and re-tear.

optionExplanations.A: The outer rim is the RED zone (vascularized).
optionExplanations.B: The red zone is peripheral at the capsular junction, not adjacent to the central femoral condyle.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Arnar vascular supply to the menisci arises from the medial and lateral genicular arteries through the perimeniscal capillary plexus. The meniscus is divided into three vascular zones: (1) Red-Red Zone (outer 10-25% / outer 1-3 mm, fully vascularized with high healing potential), (2) Red-White Zone (intermediate border, intermediate vascularity), and (3) White-White Zone (inner 60-70% / inner two-thirds, completely AVASCULAR, nourished solely by synovial fluid diffusion, with zero intrinsic healing potential).
optionExplanations.D: The inner two-thirds is the white-white avascular zone; the red zone is only the peripheral third.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the central white-white zone of the meniscus as completely avascular.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following anatomical characteristics correctly differentiates the lateral meniscus from the medial meniscus?

options.A: The lateral meniscus is loosely attached to the joint capsule interrupted by Popliteal muscle
options.B: Lateral meniscus is C-shaped and larger the medial meniscus
options.C: Lateral meniscus moves more posteriorly during knee flexion
options.D: Medial meniscus is more mobile than lateral meniscus

questions.explanation:
The lateral meniscus is circular/O-shaped, covers a larger percentage of the articular surface (~70%), and is far more MOBILE than the medial meniscus. Its peripheral capsular attachment is interrupted posterolaterally by the popliteus tendon hiatus (where the popliteus tendon passes through to insert on the lateral femoral condyle). This mobility protects it from injury compared to the firmly anchored medial meniscus.

High-yield: Medial Meniscus: C-shaped, rigidly attached to deep MCL and capsule, less mobile → Injured 3x more often. Lateral Meniscus: O-shaped/circular, separated from capsule by popliteus tendon hiatus, highly mobile → Less frequently injured.

Exam trap: Because the medial meniscus is firmly anchored to the deep medial collateral ligament, valgus-twisting injuries frequently tear the MCL and medial meniscus simultaneously.

[Review note] Option C (lateral meniscus moves more posteriorly in flexion) is also accurate. Source key A retained.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The lateral meniscus is circular/O-shaped, covers a larger percentage of the articular surface (~70%), and is far more MOBILE than the medial meniscus. Its peripheral capsular attachment is interrupted posterolaterally by the popliteus tendon hiatus (where the popliteus tendon passes through to insert on the lateral femoral condyle). This mobility protects it from injury compared to the firmly anchored medial meniscus.
optionExplanations.B: The MEDIAL meniscus is C-shaped and larger in anteroposterior diameter; the lateral meniscus is smaller and circular (O-shaped).
optionExplanations.C: This statement is also accurate in the literature (the lateral meniscus is more mobile and translates further posteriorly in flexion than the medial meniscus). The source key nevertheless selects A, so this item is flagged as possible multiple-correct.
optionExplanations.D: The LATERAL meniscus is twice as mobile as the medial meniscus (~11 mm excursion vs. ~5 mm for medial).
optionExplanations.E: The lateral meniscus is the more mobile one; the medial meniscus is the one firmly anchored to the capsule and deep MCL.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish the lateral meniscus by its greater mobility and capsular interruption by the popliteus tendon.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the medial patellofemoral ligament (MPFL)?

options.A: It is a dynamic stabilizer of the patella
options.B: It connects the medial edge of the patella to the lateral femoral epicondyle
options.C: It is static soft tissue stabilizer
options.D: It attaches to the tibial tuberosity
options.E: It prevent patella from medial dislocation

questions.explanation:
The Medial Patellofemoral Ligament (MPFL) is the primary STATIC soft tissue restraint preventing LATERAL patellar subluxation and dislocation, providing approximately 50-60% of total restraining force from 0° to 30° of knee flexion. It runs from the upper two-thirds of the medial patellar border to the femoral insertion point between the medial epicondyle and adductor tubercle (Schöttle's point).

High-yield: MPFL is torn in >90-100% of acute lateral patellar dislocations. Surgical MPFL reconstruction using a gracilis or semitendinosus autograft is indicated for recurrent patellar instability.

Exam trap: Do not confuse static stabilizers (MPFL, trochlear bony geometry) with dynamic stabilizers (VMO muscle).

optionExplanations.A: Vastus medialis obliquus (VMO) is the primary DYNAMIC stabilizer; MPFL is a passive/static ligament.
optionExplanations.B: It attaches to the MEDIAL femoral epicondyle (Schöttle's point), not the lateral epicondyle.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The Medial Patellofemoral Ligament (MPFL) is the primary STATIC soft tissue restraint preventing LATERAL patellar subluxation and dislocation, providing approximately 50-60% of total restraining force from 0° to 30° of knee flexion. It runs from the upper two-thirds of the medial patellar border to the femoral insertion point between the medial epicondyle and adductor tubercle (Schöttle's point).
optionExplanations.D: The patellar tendon attaches to the tibial tuberosity, not the MPFL.
optionExplanations.E: It prevents LATERAL patellar displacement; medial dislocations are exceedingly rare.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the MPFL as the primary static soft tissue restraint preventing lateral patellar displacement.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding acute patellar dislocation?

options.A: It is more common in males
options.B: Medial patellar dislocation is more common than lateral
options.C: The typical mechanism involves a flexed knee with valgus force (and external tibial rotation)
options.D: It usually results from a direct blow force to the knee in extension

questions.explanation:
Acute patellar dislocation almost always occurs LATERAL to the trochlea. The classic non-contact mechanism is a sudden internal rotation of the femur on a planted, externally rotated foot with the knee in slight flexion and valgus stress, accompanied by forceful quadriceps contraction. This drives the patella laterally over the lateral femoral condyle.

High-yield: Predisposing factors for lateral patellar dislocation: Trochlear dysplasia, Patella alta (high patella), Increased tibial tubercle-trochlear groove (TTTG) distance (>20 mm), and increased Q-angle.

Exam trap: Osteochondral loose body fractures (from the medial patellar facet or lateral femoral condyle) occur in up to 30-40% of dislocations and require surgical excision or fixation.

optionExplanations.A: More common in young FEMALE athletes due to greater ligamentous laxity, increased Q-angle, and femoral anteversion.
optionExplanations.B: >98% of patellar dislocations occur LATERALLY; medial dislocations are rare and usually iatrogenic.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Acute patellar dislocation almost always occurs LATERAL to the trochlea. The classic non-contact mechanism is a sudden internal rotation of the femur on a planted, externally rotated foot with the knee in slight flexion and valgus stress, accompanied by forceful quadriceps contraction. This drives the patella laterally over the lateral femoral condyle.
optionExplanations.D: Non-contact twisting flexion-valgus mechanics account for the vast majority; direct blows are less common.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the flexed knee, valgus, and external tibial rotation mechanism of acute lateral patellar dislocation.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding meniscal injuries is INCORRECT?

options.A: They may be associated with ligamentous injuries, such as ACL tears
options.B: They usually cause mechanical symptoms like locking or catching
options.C: Medial meniscus is more frequently injured than lateral meniscus
options.D: They typically present with immediate joint effusion

questions.explanation:
Because the central two-thirds of the meniscus is avascular, isolated meniscal tears do NOT cause immediate hemarthrosis. They typically present with a DELAYED effusion (serous synovitis) developing 12 to 24 hours later or insidious joint line swelling. By contrast, IMMEDIATE joint effusion/hemarthrosis (within 1-2 hours) is the classic hallmark of an acute ACL rupture or patellar dislocation.

High-yield: Timing of Effusion is High-Yield: Immediate effusion (<2 hours) = Hemarthrosis (ACL tear >70%, Patellar dislocation, Tibial plateau fracture); Delayed effusion (12-24 hours) = Meniscal tear or ligament sprain.

Exam trap: A knee that locks in flexion with an inability to reach full terminal extension indicates a bucket-handle meniscal tear requiring urgent arthroscopy.

optionExplanations.A: ACL ruptures are associated with lateral meniscus tears acutely and medial meniscus tears chronically.
optionExplanations.B: Displaced bucket-handle tears cause true mechanical joint locking (inability to fully extend the knee).
optionExplanations.C: Medial meniscus is less mobile and torn significantly more frequently in non-contact degenerative and sports settings.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Because the central two-thirds of the meniscus is avascular, isolated meniscal tears do NOT cause immediate hemarthrosis. They typically present with a DELAYED effusion (serous synovitis) developing 12 to 24 hours later or insidious joint line swelling. By contrast, IMMEDIATE joint effusion/hemarthrosis (within 1-2 hours) is the classic hallmark of an acute ACL rupture or patellar dislocation.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate the delayed effusion of meniscal tears from the immediate hemarthrosis of ACL tears.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: Which of the following is the most common secondary intra-articular injury associated with chronic, un-reconstructed ACL deficiency?
questions.explanation:
In an ACUTE ACL tear, the LATERAL meniscus is most frequently injured (~55%) due to lateral compartment impaction during the pivot-shift event. However, in CHRONIC ACL deficiency, repeated episodes of anterior tibial translation and rotatory instability repeatedly shear the posterior horn of the MEDIAL meniscus (which serves as a secondary wedge restraint to anterior translation), leading to secondary MEDIAL meniscus tears in up to 70-80% of patients over time.

High-yield: ACL Tear Meniscal Associations: Acute ACL injury → Lateral meniscus tear (#1); Chronic ACL instability → Medial meniscus tear (#1).

Exam trap: Failing to reconstruct an ACL in an active young patient leads to predictable medial meniscal tearing and early unicompartmental osteoarthritis.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. In an ACUTE ACL tear, the LATERAL meniscus is most frequently injured (~55%) due to lateral compartment impaction during the pivot-shift event. However, in CHRONIC ACL deficiency, repeated episodes of anterior tibial translation and rotatory instability repeatedly shear the posterior horn of the MEDIAL meniscus (which serves as a secondary wedge restraint to anterior translation), leading to secondary MEDIAL meniscus tears in up to 70-80% of patients over time.
optionExplanations.B: MCL injuries occur acutely from valgus impact, not as progressive chronic degenerative sequelae.
optionExplanations.C: Lateral meniscus tears dominate the acute phase, while medial meniscus tears dominate the chronic phase.
optionExplanations.D: Patellar dislocation is not a typical secondary sequela of chronic ACL deficiency; patellofemoral instability depends on trochlear dysplasia, patella alta and MPFL integrity.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify medial meniscus tears as the primary chronic complication of un-reconstructed ACL deficiency.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: A 16-year-old boy sustained a twisting injury to his knee while playing football. He was able to continue playing for the remainder of the match. However, the following morning, he woke up with significant knee joint swelling, pain with deep flexion, and localized joint line tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The scenario of an athletic twisting injury allowing continued play followed by delayed onset of swelling (next morning / 12-24 hours later) is classic for a MENISCAL TEAR. Complete ACL tears almost always force immediate cessation of play with a perceived 'pop' and tense hemarthrosis within 1-2 hours.

High-yield: Clinical contrast: ACL = 'Pop', unable to continue playing, rapid swelling (<2 hours); Meniscus = Twisting, able to finish game, delayed swelling (next morning).

Exam trap: Never dismiss a patient who finished the game; meniscal tears frequently allow ambulation until inflammatory synovitis manifests the next day.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The scenario of an athletic twisting injury allowing continued play followed by delayed onset of swelling (next morning / 12-24 hours later) is classic for a MENISCAL TEAR. Complete ACL tears almost always force immediate cessation of play with a perceived 'pop' and tense hemarthrosis within 1-2 hours.
optionExplanations.B: PCL tears result from posterior pretibial impact ('dashboard injury') or hyperflexion, causing mild swelling without delayed twisting meniscal features.

questions.educationalObjective: Diagnose meniscal tear based on twisting mechanism, continuation of play, and delayed joint effusion.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: Regarding the special orthopedic physical examination test shown in the illustration (patient supine, knee flexed to 90°, examiner sitting on the foot and translating the proximal tibia anteriorly), which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: Used for diagnosis of extraarticular ligament
options.B: The front of the foot should be free with no stabilization
options.C: It is less sensitive than the Lachman test
options.D: It is called the posterior drawer test
options.E: A positive test means weak ligament and strong quadriceps

questions.explanation:
The test depicted is the ANTERIOR DRAWER TEST for the ACL. At 90° of flexion, hamstring spasm, the posterior horn of the medial meniscus wedging against the femoral condyle, and joint hemarthrosis frequently block anterior translation, reducing the sensitivity of the anterior drawer test to ~60-70%. By contrast, the LACHMAN TEST (performed at 20-30° flexion) eliminates meniscal blocking and minimizes hamstring resistance, making it the most sensitive physical examination test for ACL rupture (>85-95% sensitivity).

High-yield: Test sensitivities for ACL: Lachman (>85-95%) > Pivot-shift (>95% specificity, pathognomonic for rotatory instability, but low sensitivity awake due to guarding) > Anterior drawer (~60-70%).

Exam trap: Always ensure the normal starting position of the tibia before an anterior drawer test; an un-recognized posterior tibial sag from a torn PCL can produce a 'false-positive' anterior drawer.

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Illustration of the anterior drawer test of the knee with the patient supine, knee at 90 degrees, foot stabilized by examiner, and hands drawing proximal tibia anteriorly.

optionExplanations.A: The ACL is an INTRA-ARTICULAR (though extrasynovial) ligament.
optionExplanations.B: The examiner MUST sit on the patient's foot to firmly stabilize it during the anterior drawer test.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The test depicted is the ANTERIOR DRAWER TEST for the ACL. At 90° of flexion, hamstring spasm, the posterior horn of the medial meniscus wedging against the femoral condyle, and joint hemarthrosis frequently block anterior translation, reducing the sensitivity of the anterior drawer test to ~60-70%. By contrast, the LACHMAN TEST (performed at 20-30° flexion) eliminates meniscal blocking and minimizes hamstring resistance, making it the most sensitive physical examination test for ACL rupture (>85-95% sensitivity).
optionExplanations.D: Translating the tibia anteriorly tests the ACL (anterior drawer); pushing it posteriorly tests the PCL (posterior drawer).
optionExplanations.E: A positive anterior drawer test indicates ACL laxity or insufficiency; it says nothing about quadriceps strength.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the anterior drawer test and understand why it is clinically less sensitive than the Lachman test.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: All of the following anatomical and clinical statements regarding the knee menisci are true EXCEPT:

options.B: Injury of the medial meniscus is more common
options.C: Anterior horn is wider than posterior
options.E: Twisting is the most common type of injury

questions.explanation:
In both the medial and lateral menisci (and especially pronounced in the medial meniscus), the POSTERIOR HORN IS SIGNIFICANTLY WIDER in the anteroposterior and coronal dimensions than the narrow anterior horn. Most weight-bearing and impact stresses are transmitted through the broader posterior horn, which is also the most common site of meniscal tearing.

High-yield: Meniscal Horn Dimensions: Posterior horn > Anterior horn in width. Tears occur most frequently in the posterior horn of the medial meniscus.

Exam trap: Do not confuse discoid meniscus (congenital variant where the lateral meniscus is a complete disc rather than a crescent, prone to snapping in children) with normal anatomy.

optionExplanations.A: The lateral meniscus has ~11 mm of excursion compared to ~5 mm for the medial meniscus.
optionExplanations.B: The medial meniscus is injured 3 times more frequently than the lateral meniscus.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. In both the medial and lateral menisci (and especially pronounced in the medial meniscus), the POSTERIOR HORN IS SIGNIFICANTLY WIDER in the anteroposterior and coronal dimensions than the narrow anterior horn. Most weight-bearing and impact stresses are transmitted through the broader posterior horn, which is also the most common site of meniscal tearing.
optionExplanations.D: The medial meniscus is semicircular or C-shaped.
optionExplanations.E: Rotational twisting under weight-bearing is the classic injury mechanism.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall that the posterior horn of the meniscus is wider than the anterior horn and is the most common tear site.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: A 25-year-old male skier sustained a high-energy twisting valgus injury to his left knee when his ski tip caught in the snow. Physical examination reveals medial joint line ecchymosis, opening to valgus stress at 30° flexion, and tenderness over the medial femoral epicondyle. Which ligament is primarily injured?
questions.explanation:
A valgus impact or twisting strain to the knee directly tensions the Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL), which is the primary static restraint to valgus displacement. Tears commonly avulse from the femoral origin at the medial epicondyle (often forming a calcified Pellegrini-Stieda lesion on late radiographs).

High-yield: Testing MCL: Valgus stress test at 30° flexion isolates the superficial MCL. Valgus stress at 0° (full extension) tests the MCL PLUS the posterior capsule and cruciate ligaments (indicates major multi-ligamentous injury if lax in extension).

Exam trap: Unlike the ACL, the MCL has excellent vascularity and healing potential; isolated Grade I, II, and even most Grade III tears heal successfully with non-operative functional hinged bracing.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A valgus impact or twisting strain to the knee directly tensions the Medial Collateral Ligament (MCL), which is the primary static restraint to valgus displacement. Tears commonly avulse from the femoral origin at the medial epicondyle (often forming a calcified Pellegrini-Stieda lesion on late radiographs).
optionExplanations.B: ACL tears result from pivot-shift internal rotation/hyperextension, tested by Lachman's.
optionExplanations.C: PCL tears result from posterior tibial translation (dashboard injury).
optionExplanations.D: Menisci cushion axial loads; isolated valgus opening is specific to the MCL.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the medial collateral ligament as the primary restraint to valgus knee stress.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: All of the following anatomical and clinical statements are TRUE regarding the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) EXCEPT:

options.B: Medial meniscus injury association is the most common meniscal injury in the acute setting
options.C: ACL reconstruction surgery is the gold standard in young patients
options.D: The tibial attachment is stronger than the femoral attachment
options.E: Primary restraint to anterior tibial translation

questions.explanation:
In the ACUTE setting of an ACL tear, a LATERAL meniscus tear is the most common associated meniscal lesion (~55-60%), resulting from lateral compartment impaction and contusion during the subluxation. Medial meniscus tears predominate in CHRONIC ACL deficiency.

High-yield: Two Bundles of the ACL: (1) Anteromedial (AM) bundle (tight in flexion, resists anterior translation), (2) Posterolateral (PL) bundle (tight in extension, resists rotational laxity).

Exam trap: Primary direct suture repair of midsubstance ACL tears has historically failed; autograft reconstruction is standard.

optionExplanations.A: Average adult ACL length is approximately 31 to 38 mm (mean ~32 mm) with width ~10-12 mm.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. In the ACUTE setting of an ACL tear, a LATERAL meniscus tear is the most common associated meniscal lesion (~55-60%), resulting from lateral compartment impaction and contusion during the subluxation. Medial meniscus tears predominate in CHRONIC ACL deficiency.
optionExplanations.C: Surgical reconstruction with autograft (bone-patellar tendon-bone or hamstrings/quadriceps) is the standard in young, active patients.
optionExplanations.D: The tibial footprint is larger and structurally stronger than the femoral origin.
optionExplanations.E: The ACL provides ~85% of total resistance to anterior tibial displacement.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that lateral meniscus tears are most common in acute ACL tears, while medial meniscus tears dominate chronic ACL instability.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: A 30-year-old male front-seat unrestrained passenger was involved in a high-speed motor vehicle collision where his flexed knee struck the vehicle dashboard. What knee structure is most commonly injured by this mechanism?
questions.explanation:
The Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL) is the primary restraint to posterior tibial translation. The classic mechanism of PCL rupture is a direct blow to the anterior proximal tibia with the knee in flexion ('dashboard injury'), driving the tibia posteriorly relative to the femur.

High-yield: Diagnostic signs of PCL rupture: (1) Posterior Sag Sign (Godfrey's test: tibia drops posteriorly under gravity at 90° flexion), (2) Posterior Drawer Test, (3) Quadriceps Active Test.

Exam trap: On initial exam, a posterior tibial sag can be mistaken for anterior displacement, leading to a misdiagnosis of an ACL tear. Always check resting tibial alignment before testing drawer!

optionExplanations.A: Torn by twisting, varus, and valgus stresses, respectively.
optionExplanations.B: ACL is injured by hyperextension or valgus-external rotation, not posterior tibial impaction.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The Posterior Cruciate Ligament (PCL) is the primary restraint to posterior tibial translation. The classic mechanism of PCL rupture is a direct blow to the anterior proximal tibia with the knee in flexion ('dashboard injury'), driving the tibia posteriorly relative to the femur.
optionExplanations.D: Torn by twisting, varus, and valgus stresses, respectively.
optionExplanations.E: Torn by twisting, varus, and valgus stresses, respectively.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the PCL as the ligament damaged in dashboard injuries with direct anterior tibial impact.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: A Segond fracture (a small vertical cortical avulsion fracture of the lateral proximal tibial plateau immediately distal to the joint line) is pathognomonic for high-grade injury to which major knee ligament?
questions.explanation:
A Segond fracture is an avulsion fracture of the anterolateral tibial plateau at the insertion of the Anterolateral Ligament (ALL) and midthird lateral capsular ligament, produced by internal rotation and varus stress during an acute pivot-shift episode. While the bony avulsion is lateral, it is pathognomonic for a concurrent rupture of the ANTERIOR CRUCIATE LIGAMENT (ACL) in >75-90% of cases.

High-yield: Segond fracture on AP knee X-ray = ACL tear (>75-90% association) + Anterolateral Ligament (ALL) disruption.

Exam trap: The Segond bone fleck is small and easily overlooked; always inspect the lateral tibial margin on AP radiographs of acutely swollen knees.

optionExplanations.A: Pellegrini-Stieda lesion represents calcification at the medial femoral epicondyle following MCL injury.
optionExplanations.B: Meniscal tears may coexist with ACL injury, but the Segond fracture is a bony avulsion of the lateral capsule/anterolateral ligament insertion that signals a concomitant ACL rupture; it is not a marker of meniscal pathology.
optionExplanations.C: LCL avulses from the fibular head (arcuate sign), not the lateral tibial plateau.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A Segond fracture is an avulsion fracture of the anterolateral tibial plateau at the insertion of the Anterolateral Ligament (ALL) and midthird lateral capsular ligament, produced by internal rotation and varus stress during an acute pivot-shift episode. While the bony avulsion is lateral, it is pathognomonic for a concurrent rupture of the ANTERIOR CRUCIATE LIGAMENT (ACL) in >75-90% of cases.
optionExplanations.E: Reverse Segond fracture (avulsion of deep medial capsular ligament off medial tibial plateau) is associated with PCL tears.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize a Segond fracture as virtually pathognomonic for an ACL rupture.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: A skyline (Merchant/axial) knee radiograph demonstrates acute lateral dislocation of the patella completely displaced off the femoral trochlea. Which of the following is the CORRECT immediate management step in the Emergency Room?

options.A: Emergent reduction and immobilization should be done at the ER
options.B: Usually happens from direct contact trauma
options.C: Internal tibial torsion predisposes to this injury
options.D: Always requires surgical reconstruction to prevent recurrence
options.E: Medial patellofemoral ligament is rarely torn

questions.explanation:
Acute lateral patellar dislocation requires prompt bedside closed reduction in the Emergency Room. Closed reduction is easily performed by gently extending the knee while applying medially directed pressure to the lateral aspect of the patella. Following reduction, the knee is immobilized in a knee immobilizer or hinged brace locked in extension for comfort, followed by early functional rehabilitation.

High-yield: Patellar Reduction Technique: Gentle knee extension + gentle medial push on the lateral patellar border. Anesthesia/sedation may be given for comfort.

Exam trap: Always obtain post-reduction radiographs and MRI to rule out osteochondral shear fractures of the patella or lateral femoral condyle.

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Axial/skyline radiographs showing an abnormal image with the patella completely dislocated laterally compared to a normal centered patella in the trochlear groove.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Acute lateral patellar dislocation requires prompt bedside closed reduction in the Emergency Room. Closed reduction is easily performed by gently extending the knee while applying medially directed pressure to the lateral aspect of the patella. Following reduction, the knee is immobilized in a knee immobilizer or hinged brace locked in extension for comfort, followed by early functional rehabilitation.
optionExplanations.B: Most cases (>80%) occur from non-contact twisting injuries with quadriceps contraction.
optionExplanations.C: EXTERNAL tibial torsion and increased Q-angle predispose to lateral dislocation.
optionExplanations.D: First-time dislocations without osteochondral fractures are managed conservatively; surgery is reserved for loose bodies or recurrent instability.
optionExplanations.E: The MPFL is torn in the vast majority of acute lateral dislocations.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify prompt closed reduction and knee immobilization as the primary emergency management of acute patellar dislocation.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: All of the following statements are true regarding a pediatric lateral condyle fracture of the distal humerus EXCEPT:

options.B: Treatment is by cast above elbow
options.E: It could be an avulsion fracture

questions.explanation:
Lateral condyle fractures are intra-articular and unstable due to forearm extensor pull. Displaced fractures cannot be managed with simple casting; they require operative reduction and percutaneous pin fixation.

High-yield: Lateral condyle fracture is a Salter-Harris IV equivalent fracture passing across the ossified capitellum into the unossified trochlea.

Exam trap: Do not confuse lateral epicondyle avulsions (extra-articular, rare) with lateral condyle fractures (intra-articular, common, high risk).

optionExplanations.A: Comparison radiographs of the normal contralateral elbow are essential to interpret unossified pediatric epiphyseal centers.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Lateral condyle fractures are intra-articular and unstable due to forearm extensor pull. Displaced fractures cannot be managed with simple casting; they require operative reduction and percutaneous pin fixation.
optionExplanations.C: Displacement is frequent due to extensor muscle traction and joint fluid bathing.
optionExplanations.D: It traverses the articular cartilage into the trochlea (Milch Type I or II).
optionExplanations.E: Can occur via avulsion by the lateral collateral ligament and extensor origin or shear from radial head impaction.

questions.educationalObjective: Confirm that simple cast immobilization is inappropriate for displaced lateral condyle fractures.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: All of the following statements regarding the ACL are true EXCEPT:

options.A: The tibial attachment is weaker than femoral
options.B: Primary restraint to anterior tibial translation
options.D: ACL repair has high risk of failure
options.E: Lateral meniscus injury is the most common associated injury

questions.explanation:
The tibial insertion footprint of the ACL is approximately 120% LARGER and structurally STRONGER than the femoral footprint. Failure in midsubstance or femoral avulsion occurs far more easily than tibial footprint failure in adults (though tibial spine avulsion can occur in children before skeletal maturity). Stating that the tibial attachment is weaker is false.

High-yield: In children, open physes make bone weaker than ligament → ACL trauma produces a Tibial Spine (Eminence) Avulsion fracture (Meyers & McKeever classification) rather than a midsubstance ligament tear.

Exam trap: Tibial eminence avulsions are treated with closed reduction or arthroscopic suture/screw fixation, NOT tendon reconstruction.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The tibial insertion footprint of the ACL is approximately 120% LARGER and structurally STRONGER than the femoral footprint. Failure in midsubstance or femoral avulsion occurs far more easily than tibial footprint failure in adults (though tibial spine avulsion can occur in children before skeletal maturity). Stating that the tibial attachment is weaker is false.
optionExplanations.B: ACL provides ~85% of total resistance to anterior tibial translation.
optionExplanations.C: Normal length is 31-38 mm.
optionExplanations.D: Primary suture repair carries failure rates up to 40-50%; reconstruction with tendon autograft is required.
optionExplanations.E: Lateral meniscus tear is the most common meniscal injury in acute ACL tears.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that the tibial insertion footprint of the ACL is larger and stronger than its femoral origin.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: Regarding this radiograph of a long-bone fracture, which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: Radial nerve is likely affected; it will cause wrist drop
options.B: Anatomical exposure (what should be shown in X-ray) is acceptable
options.D: Shaft is angulated in varus deformity

questions.explanation:
Angular alignment is described by the direction of the distal fragment relative to the proximal shaft. In a varus deformity, the distal fragment is tilted toward the midline (or the apex points away from the midline/lateral). The radiograph demonstrates a classic varus malalignment.

High-yield: Varus vs. Valgus: Varus = Distal segment tilted towards midline (Apex lateral); Valgus = Distal segment tilted away from midline (Apex medial).

Exam trap: Always specify whether you are describing 'apex angulation' or 'distal fragment alignment' to prevent communication errors.

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): Long-bone radiograph demonstrating diaphyseal fracture with apex directed laterally, corresponding to a varus (medial tilt of distal segment) angular deformity.

optionExplanations.A: Palsy depends on specific anatomical nerve pathways and cannot be assumed without clinical deficit.
optionExplanations.B: Fails the rule of two if adjacent joints are not included.
optionExplanations.C: Penetration adequately visualizes cortical borders.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Angular alignment is described by the direction of the distal fragment relative to the proximal shaft. In a varus deformity, the distal fragment is tilted toward the midline (or the apex points away from the midline/lateral). The radiograph demonstrates a classic varus malalignment.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify varus angular deformity on plain radiography of long-bone fractures.

questions.section: Chapter 7: Knee Sports Injuries & Ligamentous Pathology
questions.question: In patients with hip disease (such as Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis, Legg-Calvé-Perthes, or hip osteoarthritis), hip pathology frequently refers pain exclusively to the ipsilateral knee through which shared neural pathway?
questions.explanation:
The Obturator Nerve (L2, L3, L4 anterior divisions) provides sensory articular innervation to the hip joint capsule as well as the knee joint capsule and medial thigh/distal knee skin. Sensory convergence in the lumbosacral dorsal horn causes pain originating in the hip to be perceived as isolated knee pain (Howship-Romberg phenomenon / referred pain). In adolescents presenting with isolated knee pain, examining the hip is mandatory to avoid missing SCFE.

High-yield: A child or adolescent presenting with isolated knee pain or a painless limp has SCFE or Perthes disease of the HIP until proven otherwise via bilateral hip radiographs (AP and Frog-leg lateral).

Exam trap: Never radiograph ONLY the knee in an adolescent with knee pain; missed SCFE leads to femoral head avascular necrosis and permanent disability.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The Obturator Nerve (L2, L3, L4 anterior divisions) provides sensory articular innervation to the hip joint capsule as well as the knee joint capsule and medial thigh/distal knee skin. Sensory convergence in the lumbosacral dorsal horn causes pain originating in the hip to be perceived as isolated knee pain (Howship-Romberg phenomenon / referred pain). In adolescents presenting with isolated knee pain, examining the hip is mandatory to avoid missing SCFE.
optionExplanations.B: Superior gluteal nerve innervates gluteus medius/minimus without cutaneous/knee sensory branches.
optionExplanations.C: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve causes meralgia paresthetica (lateral thigh burning).
optionExplanations.D: Sciatic nerve radiates down the posterior thigh and calf/foot.
optionExplanations.E: There is no 'popliteal nerve' linking the hip and knee joints (the sciatic nerve divides into the tibial and common peroneal nerves in the popliteal fossa). The shared sensory pathway is the obturator nerve.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the obturator nerve as the anatomical mediator of hip pain referred to the knee.

questions.section: Chapter 8: Pediatric Orthopedics: Hip & Foot Disorders
questions.question: A 6-week-old infant is brought for a routine well-child checkup. Physical examination demonstrates a positive Ortolani test (a palpable, audible 'clunk' of reduction as the flexed hip is gently abducted). What is the definitive diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The Ortolani maneuver tests for a dislocated hip that is reducible: with the infant relaxed and supine, the examiner flexes the hips to 90°, places fingers over the greater trochanter, and gently abducts while applying an anterior lifting force. A palpable 'clunk' occurs as the dislocated femoral head slides back into the acetabular socket, confirming the diagnosis of Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH).

High-yield: Barlow vs. Ortolani: Barlow = Dislocates a dislocatable hip ('B = Bad / Dislocates Out'); Ortolani = Reduces a dislocated hip ('O = Out to In /Reduces').

Exam trap: Benign high-pitched ligamentous 'clicks' are normal and common; a positive Ortolani is a deep, palpable 'clunk' of true reduction.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The Ortolani maneuver tests for a dislocated hip that is reducible: with the infant relaxed and supine, the examiner flexes the hips to 90°, places fingers over the greater trochanter, and gently abducts while applying an anterior lifting force. A palpable 'clunk' occurs as the dislocated femoral head slides back into the acetabular socket, confirming the diagnosis of Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH).
optionExplanations.B: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head occurring in children aged 4 to 8 years.
optionExplanations.C: SCFE is displacement of the femoral head epiphysis through the growth plate in obese adolescents aged 11 to 14 years.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify a positive Ortolani sign as diagnostic of Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip in neonates.

questions.section: Chapter 8: Pediatric Orthopedics: Hip & Foot Disorders
questions.question: In an infant aged 2 to 3 months presenting with developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), after soft tissue contractures have developed around the dislocated joint, what is the most sensitive and common clinical physical finding?
questions.explanation:
While Ortolani and Barlow tests are sensitive in the first 4 to 6 weeks of life, after 2 to 3 months of age, secondary soft tissue contractures (especially of the adductor longus and iliopsoas) develop around the chronically displaced femoral head. Consequently, the hip becomes fixed in a dislocated position and cannot be reduced with an Ortolani clunk. The single most sensitive and reliable clinical sign of DDH in infants aged >2-3 months is ASYMMETRICAL LIMITATION OF HIP ABDUCTION (<60° of abduction when hips are flexed to 90°).

High-yield: Evolution of DDH Signs: <3 months = Ortolani and Barlow tests; >3 months = Limited hip abduction (most reliable) and positive Galeazzi sign (apparent femoral shortening).

Exam trap: Asymmetric thigh skin folds have low specificity; asymmetric hip abduction is far more reliable.

optionExplanations.A: The limb is SHORTENED (Galeazzi sign), never elongated.
optionExplanations.B: Limping is not observable in non-ambulatory 2-3 month infants.
optionExplanations.C: Shortening involves the FEMUR, not the tibia (Galeazzi test shows knee height discrepancy due to femoral displacement).
optionExplanations.D: Correct. While Ortolani and Barlow tests are sensitive in the first 4 to 6 weeks of life, after 2 to 3 months of age, secondary soft tissue contractures (especially of the adductor longus and iliopsoas) develop around the chronically displaced femoral head. Consequently, the hip becomes fixed in a dislocated position and cannot be reduced with an Ortolani clunk. The single most sensitive and reliable clinical sign of DDH in infants aged >2-3 months is ASYMMETRICAL LIMITATION OF HIP ABDUCTION (<60° of abduction when hips are flexed to 90°).

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize limited hip abduction as the most sensitive physical examination sign of DDH in infants older than 2-3 months.

questions.section: Chapter 8: Pediatric Orthopedics: Hip & Foot Disorders
questions.question: Which of the following pediatric foot abnormalities is most characteristically and frequently associated with underlying neuromuscular disorders (such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease or spinal dysraphism)?
questions.explanation:
Pes cavus (an abnormally high medial longitudinal arch) is pathological until proven otherwise. Over 60-80% of bilateral pes cavus cases are secondary to underlying neuromuscular diseases, most notably Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT / hereditary motor sensory neuropathy), Friedreich's ataxia, spinal dysraphism (tethered cord), or cerebral palsy. Muscle imbalance (peroneus longus overpowering anterior tibialis, and posterior tibialis overpowering peroneus brevis) drives plantarflexion of the first metatarsal and hindfoot varus.

High-yield: Coleman Block Test: Evaluates hindfoot flexibility in pes cavus. If hindfoot varus corrects when the 1st metatarsal hangs off a wooden block, the hindfoot is flexible, meaning the deformity is driven by a plantarflexed forefoot.

Exam trap: Any child presenting with unilateral or progressive pes cavus mandates a full neurological examination and whole-spine MRI to rule out spinal cord tethering or syrinx.

optionExplanations.A: Flexible flat foot (pes planus) is a benign normal physiological variant in young children.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Pes cavus (an abnormally high medial longitudinal arch) is pathological until proven otherwise. Over 60-80% of bilateral pes cavus cases are secondary to underlying neuromuscular diseases, most notably Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT / hereditary motor sensory neuropathy), Friedreich's ataxia, spinal dysraphism (tethered cord), or cerebral palsy. Muscle imbalance (peroneus longus overpowering anterior tibialis, and posterior tibialis overpowering peroneus brevis) drives plantarflexion of the first metatarsal and hindfoot varus.
optionExplanations.C: Congenital vertical talus causes a rigid rocker-bottom flatfoot deformity.
optionExplanations.D: CTEV (Clubfoot) is primarily an idiopathic congenital structural deformity present at birth.

questions.educationalObjective: Associate pes cavus with underlying neuromuscular disease, especially Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.

questions.section: Chapter 8: Pediatric Orthopedics: Hip & Foot Disorders
questions.question: What is the most appropriate management for an asymptomatic, flexible pes planus (flatfoot) in a healthy 4-year-old child?
questions.explanation:
Flexible flatfoot (loss of the medial longitudinal arch on weight-bearing that reconstitutes when standing on tiptoes or with great toe extension /Jack's test) is a completely normal physiological variant present in virtually all infants and young children due to ligamentous laxity and plantar fat pads. The arch naturally develops throughout the first decade of life. For asymptomatic flexible pes planus, parental education, reassurance, and observation are the only required management.

High-yield: Jack's Test (Great Toe Extension / Windlass Test): Passive dorsiflexion of the hallux tightens the plantar fascia and reconstitutes the medial longitudinal arch, proving the flatfoot is FLEXIBLE, not rigid.

Exam trap: Do not order expensive custom orthotics for asymptomatic flexible flatfeet; they do not alter natural history.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Flexible flatfoot (loss of the medial longitudinal arch on weight-bearing that reconstitutes when standing on tiptoes or with great toe extension /Jack's test) is a completely normal physiological variant present in virtually all infants and young children due to ligamentous laxity and plantar fat pads. The arch naturally develops throughout the first decade of life. For asymptomatic flexible pes planus, parental education, reassurance, and observation are the only required management.
optionExplanations.B: Custom arch supports and corrective shoes have been conclusively proven NOT to alter arch development in randomized trials and cause unnecessary parental expense.
optionExplanations.C: Surgery (calcaneal osteotomy, arthroereisis) is contraindicated in asymptomatic flexible children.
optionExplanations.D: Formal physical therapy is unnecessary unless Achilles tendon contracture is present.

questions.educationalObjective: Manage asymptomatic flexible pediatric flatfoot with reassurance and observation.

questions.section: Chapter 8: Pediatric Orthopedics: Hip & Foot Disorders
questions.question: A 13-year-old boy presents with painful, rigid flatfoot and hindfoot stiffness after joining a track team. On examination, the subtalar joint has zero inversion/eversion mobility, and the arch does not reconstitute on tiptoe standing. What is the most common underlying cause?
questions.explanation:
Tarsal coalition is an abnormal congenital fibrous, cartilaginous, or bony bridge connecting two or more tarsal bones. The two most common forms are Calcaneonavicular coalition (ages 8-12, 'anteater nose' sign on 45° internal oblique X-ray) and Talocalcaneal coalition (ages 12-16, 'C-sign' on lateral X-ray). As the coalition ossifies in adolescence, subtalar motion is completely lost, presenting as a painful, rigid flatfoot with peroneal muscle spasm (peroneal spastic flatfoot).

High-yield: Rigid Flatfoot Differential: Tarsal Coalition (adolescents, peroneal spasm, restricted subtalar motion) vs. Congenital Vertical Talus (infants, rigid rocker-bottom).

Exam trap: CT scan of the foot is the definitive imaging modality to map tarsal coalitions and assess percentage of articular surface involvement for surgical planning.

optionExplanations.C: Correct. Tarsal coalition is an abnormal congenital fibrous, cartilaginous, or bony bridge connecting two or more tarsal bones. The two most common forms are Calcaneonavicular coalition (ages 8-12, 'anteater nose' sign on 45° internal oblique X-ray) and Talocalcaneal coalition (ages 12-16, 'C-sign' on lateral X-ray). questions.educationalObjective: Identify tarsal coalition as the primary cause of painful, rigid flatfoot in adolescents.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding flexible pes planus (flatfoot) in children?
questions.explanation:
Flexible flatfoot is an extraordinarily common normal developmental variation present in up to 90% of toddlers and gradually resolving in the majority by age 10 as medial arch ligaments tighten.

High-yield: Tiptoe test differentiates flexible from rigid: Flexible flatfoot reconstitutes arch on tiptoes; Rigid flatfoot stays flat and stiff.

Exam trap: Do not treat flexible asymptomatic flatfoot aggressively; it is a normal physiological condition.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an established risk factor for Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH)?
questions.explanation:
Established risk factors for DDH reflect factors that crowd the intrauterine environment or increase ligamentous laxity in the third trimester: Breech presentation (strongest single risk factor), Female sex (80% of cases, due to circulating maternal relaxin sensitivity), First-born status (tight primigravid uterus), Family history/genetics, and Oligohydramnios. PREMATURITY is NOT a risk factor for DDH; in fact, premature infants leave the cramped intrauterine environment earlier, decreasing packaging deformation risks.

Exam trap: Prematurity is NOT a risk factor for DDH. Do not choose prematurity as a predisposing factor.

questions.question: What is the universally accepted gold standard first-line treatment for idiopathic Congenital Talipes Equinovarus (CTEV /Clubfoot)?
questions.explanation:
The Ponseti method of serial manipulation and casting is the gold standard, achieving >90-95% success rates. It involves weekly gentle manipulation around the talar head and serial above-knee plaster casting to correct the deformities in the specific anatomical sequence 'CAVE': (1) Cavus corrected by elevating the first metatarsal to align the forefoot with the hindfoot, (2) Adductus and Varus corrected by abducting the foot in supination using the lateral talar head as a fulcrum, and (3) Equinus corrected by percutaneous Achilles tenotomy (required in ~85-90% of cases).

High-yield: Correction sequence in Ponseti: Mnemonic 'CAVE' - Cavus first, then Adductus, Varus, and finally Equinus (with percutaneous tenotomy).

Exam trap: Never touch the calcaneus during Ponseti abduction; the talar head is the ONLY fulcrum. Touching the calcaneus blocks subtalar rotation.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The Ponseti method of serial manipulation and casting is the gold standard, achieving >90-95% success rates. It involves weekly gentle manipulation around the talar head and serial above-knee plaster casting to correct the deformities in the specific anatomical sequence 'CAVE': (1) Cavus corrected by elevating the first metatarsal to align the forefoot with the hindfoot, (2) Adductus and Varus corrected by abducting the foot in supination using the lateral talar head as a fulcrum, and (3) Equinus corrected by percutaneous Achilles tenotomy (required in ~85-90% of cases).
optionExplanations.B: Extensive open surgical release (posteromedial release) results in severe stiffness, pain, and arthritis, and has been largely abandoned in favor of the Ponseti method.

questions.educationalObjective: Select the Ponseti method of serial casting as first-line treatment for congenital clubfoot.

questions.question: In the conservative and multimodal management of chronic plantar fasciitis and heel pain, which of the following therapeutic options is FALSE / inappropriate?
questions.explanation:
Wearing completely flat shoes (such as flip-flops, ballet flats, or barefoot walking) places maximum tensile strain on the Achilles tendon and plantar fascia, dramatically worsening plantar fasciitis. Patients should be advised to wear supportive shoes with a cushioned heel and a SLIGHT HEEL ELEVATION (1-1.5 inches / ~2-3 cm) to unload the Achilles tendon and plantar fascia.

High-yield: Shoewear recommendation for plantar fasciitis: Supportive running shoes with rigid heel counters and slight heel lift, NEVER flat unsupportive shoes.

Exam trap: Do not inject corticosteroids directly into the plantar fat pad; it can cause irreversible fat pad atrophy and severe intractable heel bone pain.

optionExplanations.A: Extracorporeal Shock Wave Therapy (ESWT) is proven effective for recalcitrant plantar fasciitis failing 6 months of conservative care.

Patients should be advised to wear supportive shoes with a cushioned heel and a SLIGHT HEEL ELEVATION (1-1.5 inches / ~2-3 cm) to unload the Achilles tendon and plantar fascia.

questions.question: A 27-year-old patient sustained a displaced femoral neck fracture and undergoes urgent ORIF. What is the most common prevalent complication after this injury?
questions.explanation:
Osteonecrosis (AVN) is the primary complication following displaced femoral neck fractures.

High-yield: Blood supply to the femoral head: Medial femoral circumflex artery → Lateral epiphyseal branches. Torn in displaced femoral neck fractures.

Exam trap: Urgent anatomic reduction (<6 hours) in young adults reduces, but does not eliminate, the risk of osteonecrosis.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Osteonecrosis (AVN) is the primary complication following displaced femoral neck fractures.
optionExplanations.B: Hip instability/dislocation is characteristic of hip arthroplasty, not native femoral neck ORIF.
optionExplanations.C: Abductor lurch occurs with superior gluteal nerve palsy or nonunion of the greater trochanter.
optionExplanations.D: Flexion contracture is not the characteristic complication of a displaced femoral neck fracture. Disruption of the retinacular vessels makes osteonecrosis the most prevalent complication.
optionExplanations.E: Nonunion is a major complication (15-30%), but osteonecrosis (AVN) is the most prevalent and dreaded ischemic sequela.

questions.educationalObjective: Confirm osteonecrosis as the most common major complication of displaced femoral neck fractures.

questions.question: All of the following are established epidemiological risk factors and clinical associations for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease EXCEPT:
questions.explanation:
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (idiopathic osteonecrosis of the femoral head in children aged 4-8) characteristically affects boys who are SMALL FOR AGE, with SHORT STATURE and significantly DELAYED BONE AGE. Large size / tall stature is the exact opposite of the Perthes physical phenotype (tall, large, obese adolescents are prone to SCFE, not Perthes).

High-yield: Perthes Phenotype: Male (4:1), age 4-8 years, hyperactive/ADHD, short stature with delayed bone age, painless antalgic limp.

Exam trap: Contrast: Perthes = Small, short boy, age 4-8; SCFE = Large, tall/obese adolescent, age 11-14.

optionExplanations.E: Delayed skeletal maturation (bone age delayed by 1-2 years) is a classic finding.

questions.question: All of the following statements are true regarding the clinical presentation of Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease EXCEPT:

options.A: History of transient hip synovitis preceded the disease
options.C: Pain in groin, thigh, and knee
options.D: Maximum hip pain in internal rotation
options.E: Limping is usually painless and continues

questions.explanation:
While Perthes can occasionally present with an insidious mild limp, the classic presentation is an INTERMITTENT antalgic limp that is aggravated by strenuous physical activity and worse at the end of the day, accompanied by aching pain in the groin, anterior thigh, or referred to the knee. Describing the limp as universally 'painless and continuous' is inaccurate.

High-yield: Four Radiographic Stages of Perthes (Waldenström Classification): (1) Initial/Avascular necrosis (small ossific nucleus, joint space widening), (2) Fragmentation (resorption, crescent sign), (3) Reossification (healing), (4) Remodeling (healed residual deformity).

Exam trap: Early plain radiographs may show only a subtle subchondral radiolucent fracture line ('crescent sign of Caffey') best seen on frog-leg lateral view.

[Review note] Key E claims a painless continuing limp is false, but a painless limp is the classic teaching for Perthes; option B ('None is true') is also a false statement in an EXCEPT stem. Source note says the limp is intermittent and activity-related. Source key retained.

optionExplanations.B: Statements A, C and D are presented as true in the source, so 'none is true' is itself false. Together with option E this creates ambiguity in the EXCEPT stem (see review note).
optionExplanations.C: Referred pain to the thigh and knee via the obturator nerve is classic.
optionExplanations.D: Internal rotation and abduction are the earliest and most severely restricted movements.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Describing the limp as universally 'painless and continuous' is inaccurate.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that children with Perthes disease develop an activity-related antalgic limp and restricted internal rotation.

questions.question: All of the following anatomical and pathological findings are characteristic features of Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH) EXCEPT:

options.B: Acetabular labrum enlarged along superior, posterior, and inferior rim (inverted limbus)

questions.explanation:
In DDH, the femoral head dislocates SUPERIORLY and POSTERIORLY (or posterolaterally) into the false acetabulum on the ilium, NOT anteriorly. Secondary mechanical blocks to closed reduction include: (1) Pulvinar (hypertrophied fibrofatty tissue filling the true acetabular fossa), (2) Inverted acetabular labrum (limbus), (3) Hypertrophied ligamentum teres, (4) Transverse acetabular ligament pulled superiorly, and (5) Hourglass constriction of the joint capsule by the psoas tendon.

High-yield: Anatomical Obstacles to Reduction in DDH: 'P-I-L-T-H' = Pulvinar, Inverted labrum (limbus), Ligamentum teres, Transverse acetabular ligament, Hourglass capsule (psoas tendon).

Exam trap: The limbus is the inverted, hypertrophic fibrocartilaginous labrum; it prevents concentric closed reduction and may require open operative clearance.
