questions.question: A 13-year-old boy presents with left hip pain, an antalgic limp, and an externally rotated foot posture. He is diagnosed with Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE). Which of the following statements is NOT a characteristic feature of SCFE?

options.A: Most children have an open triradiate cartilage
options.B: Usually below age of 10 years for both sexes
options.D: Left side more than right side

questions.explanation:
SCFE is an adolescent disorder of the adolescent growth spurt, characteristically occurring between ages 11 to 14 in boys and ages 10 to 12 in girls (during the period of peak skeletal growth velocity when the physis is widened and mechanically vulnerable to shear stresses). Developing SCFE below the age of 10 is rare and should trigger immediate evaluation for underlying endocrine disorders (hypothyroidism, panhypopituitarism, growth hormone deficiency, renal osteodystrophy).

High-yield: Radiographic Signs of SCFE: (1) Klein's line does not intersect the lateral epiphysis on AP view (Trethowan's sign), (2) Steel's blanch sign (double density from posterior slip), (3) Epiphyseal flattening.

Exam trap: SCFE occurring in a child <10 years or >16 years, or in a patient with thin/normal BMI, demands thyroid function tests (TSH/free T4) and renal workup.

optionExplanations.A: Active open triradiate cartilage correlates with peak growth spurt and high risk for physeal slip.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Developing SCFE below the age of 10 is rare and should trigger immediate evaluation for underlying endocrine disorders (hypothyroidism, panhypopituitarism, growth hormone deficiency, renal osteodystrophy).

questions.question: All of the following are recognized physical examination findings in infants and walking children with untreated Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH) EXCEPT:
questions.explanation:
In DDH, the femoral head dislocates superiorly and posteriorly on the iliac wing, resulting in APPARENT SHORTENING of the affected lower extremity (positive Galeazzi / Allis sign). The limb is NEVER lengthened.

High-yield: Galeazzi Sign: Patient supine with hips flexed to 45° and knees flexed to 90° with feet flat on the table; the knee on the dislocated side sits lower due to femoral shortening.

Exam trap: DDH does NOT delay walking age! A child who walks at 12 months can still have severe unilateral hip dysplasia.

optionExplanations.C: Unilateral dislocation produces a positive Trendelenburg gait due to shortened hip abductor lever arm.
optionExplanations.D: Bilateral dislocation produces a classic bilateral 'waddling' duck-like gait and hyperlordosis.
optionExplanations.E: Children with DDH typically achieve independent walking at the normal expected developmental age (~12-14 months).

questions.educationalObjective: Identify limb shortening (not lengthening) as the anatomical physical finding in unilateral DDH.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognized risk factor or characteristic feature of Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease?

questions.question: All of the following statements regarding Pes Cavus (high-arched foot) are TRUE EXCEPT:

options.B: Spinal examination and imaging are part of the investigations
options.C: Most cases associated with neuromuscular diseases
options.D: Can be due to partially corrected club foot

questions.explanation:
Pes cavus is fundamentally a SECONDARY structural manifestation of underlying progressive or static neuromuscular disorders (in up to 80% of patients), such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth, Friedrich ataxia, spinal cord tethering, syringomyelia, or diastematomyelia. It is NOT typically an isolated benign 'familial' trait. Dismissing pes cavus as benign familial without performing a complete neurological workup and spine imaging risks missing treatable spinal cord lesions.

High-yield: The 'Peek-a-boo heel' sign: Looking at the patient from the front, if the medial heel is visible, it confirms hindfoot varus associated with pes cavus.

Exam trap: Never label pes cavus as 'familial' without a detailed neurological and spinal evaluation.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Pes cavus is fundamentally a SECONDARY structural manifestation of underlying progressive or static neuromuscular disorders (in up to 80% of patients), such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth, Friedrich ataxia, spinal cord tethering, syringomyelia, or diastematomyelia. It is NOT typically an isolated benign 'familial' trait. Dismissing pes cavus as benign familial without performing a complete neurological workup and spine imaging risks missing treatable spinal cord lesions.

questions.question: All of the following are recognized complications resulting from the natural history or surgical treatment (in situ cannulated screw fixation) of Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) EXCEPT:
questions.explanation:
In SCFE, the femoral neck displaces anteriorly and superiorly relative to the epiphysis, causing relative SHORTENING of the lower extremity. The limb is never lengthened. Complications of SCFE and its treatment include: (1) Avascular Necrosis (AVN, up to 50% in unstable slips), (2) Chondrolysis (rapid cartilage loss due to pin penetration into the joint), (3) Subtrochanteric femoral fracture (due to stress riser from screw entry hole placed below the lesser trochanter), and (4) Slip progression.

High-yield: Stable vs. Unstable SCFE (Loder Classification): Stable = Able to bear weight (AVN risk <5%); Unstable = Inability to bear weight even with crutches (AVN risk 25-50%).

Exam trap: Never perform forceful closed reduction of a chronic SCFE; forceful manipulation damages remaining retinacular vessels and causes catastrophic AVN.

optionExplanations.A: Subtrochanteric fracture is a major technical complication if screw entry is too low.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. In SCFE, the femoral neck displaces anteriorly and superiorly relative to the epiphysis, causing relative SHORTENING of the lower extremity. The limb is never lengthened. Complications of SCFE and its treatment include: (1) Avascular Necrosis (AVN, up to 50% in unstable slips), (2) Chondrolysis (rapid cartilage loss due to pin penetration into the joint), (3) Subtrochanteric femoral fracture (due to stress riser from screw entry hole placed below the lesser trochanter), and (4) Slip progression.
optionExplanations.C: Chondrolysis occurs if screws violate the articular cartilage (pin penetration).
optionExplanations.D: AVN is the most dreaded complication, especially in unstable SCFE (inability to bear weight even with crutches).
optionExplanations.E: Inadequate thread purchase across the physis can allow slip progression.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize AVN, chondrolysis, and subtrochanteric fracture as complications of SCFE, excluding limb lengthening.

questions.question: In a 6-month-old infant presenting for evaluation of suspected unilateral Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH), what is the most sensitive and specific clinical examination sign?
questions.explanation:
By 6 months of age, contracture of the hip adductor muscles (adductor longus) makes ASYMMETRIC LIMITATION OF HIP ABDUCTION (<50-60° on the affected side) the single most sensitive and specific clinical sign of DDH. Ortolani and Barlow tests are uniformly negative at this age because the dislocated hip has become fixed.

High-yield: At 6 months of age, the femoral head begins to ossify; therefore, AP Pelvis Radiograph (measuring acetabular index and Hilgenreiner/Perkin lines) replaces Ultrasound as the primary imaging modality.

Exam trap: In bilateral DDH, both the Galeazzi test and skin folds will appear symmetrical; only BILATERAL limitation of abduction (<50° bilaterally) alerts the physician.

optionExplanations.A: Galeazzi test (apparent femoral shortening) is a valuable sign of unilateral dislocation, but can be negative in bilateral DDH and is less specific than restricted abduction.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. By 6 months of age, contracture of the hip adductor muscles (adductor longus) makes ASYMMETRIC LIMITATION OF HIP ABDUCTION (<50-60° on the affected side) the single most sensitive and specific clinical sign of DDH. Ortolani and Barlow tests are uniformly negative at this age because the dislocated hip has become fixed.

questions.question: A 6-week-old female infant with a positive Barlow sign is diagnosed with developmental dysplasia of the hip confirmed by dynamic ultrasound (Graf Type IIb/III). What is the definitive initial management step?
questions.explanation:
The Pavlik harness is the undisputed gold standard first-line dynamic splint for infants under 6 months of age with reducible DDH. It maintains the hips in FLEXION (90-100°) and controlled ABDUCTION (45-60°), directing the femoral head directly toward the triradiate cartilage of the acetabulum to stimulate normal concentric acetabular remodeling, with success rates >90%.

High-yield: Pavlik Harness Complications: (1) Excessive Flexion (>110°) → Femoral nerve palsy (causes loss of active knee extension); (2) Excessive Abduction (>70°) → Avascular necrosis (tamponade of circumflex vessels).

Exam trap: Always examine active knee extension (quadriceps function) at every follow-up visit to rule out femoral nerve palsy from hyperflexion in a Pavlik harness.

optionExplanations.A: Delaying treatment for 4 weeks allows adductor contractures to develop, converting a reducible hip into an irreducible dislocation.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The Pavlik harness is the undisputed gold standard first-line dynamic splint for infants under 6 months of age with reducible DDH. It maintains the hips in FLEXION (90-100°) and controlled ABDUCTION (45-60°), directing the femoral head directly toward the triradiate cartilage of the acetabulum to stimulate normal concentric acetabular remodeling, with success rates >90%.

questions.question: All of the following are established clinical risk factors for Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip (DDH) EXCEPT:

options.E: Cesarean section delivery (associated with breech indication)

questions.explanation:
Prematurity is not a risk factor for DDH.

High-yield: Breech positioning prevents normal fetal leg movements and keeps hips extended/adducted in late gestation, making it the strongest risk factor for DDH.

Exam trap: Remember that breech presentation carries high risk regardless of whether delivery was vaginal or via Cesarean section.

optionExplanations.E: Cesarean delivery is a marker of the breech indication rather than an independent cause; the risk comes from breech presentation regardless of delivery mode, so the source treats this as an accepted risk-factor context.

questions.question: All of the following are established risk factors and clinical associations for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease EXCEPT:
questions.explanation:
Large size is not a risk factor for Perthes disease; affected children are small with delayed bone age.

High-yield: Head-at-Risk Signs in Perthes (Catterall): (1) Gage's sign (V-shaped radiolucency in lateral epiphysis), (2) Calcification lateral to epiphysis, (3) Lateral subluxation of femoral head, (4) Horizontal growth plate, (5) Diffuse metaphyseal reaction.

Exam trap: Lateral subluxation of the femoral head is the most critical head-at-risk sign; it indicates loss of containment requiring surgical containment osteotomy (varus derotation osteotomy or Salter innominate osteotomy).

optionExplanations.B: Increased mechanical joint loading is associated with Perthes progression.
optionExplanations.C: Sickle cell anemia and thalassemias cause secondary osteonecrosis indistinguishable from Perthes.
optionExplanations.D: ADHD and hyperactive physical behavior are strongly associated with Perthes (~30% of cases).

questions.question: Which of the following clinical findings or history elements is considered a definitive 'Red Flag' in the evaluation of low back pain, requiring urgent advanced imaging?

options.C: Stiffness in the morning for < 30 mm

questions.explanation:
Unexplained weight loss in a patient presenting with low back pain is a critical red flag indicating potential underlying malignancy (metastasis, multiple myeloma, lymphoma) or chronic systemic spinal infection (tuberculous spondylodiscitis / Pott's disease). It mandates immediate investigation with ESR/CRP and spinal MRI.

High-yield: Red Flags for Low Back Pain (Mnemonic 'TUNA FISH'): Trauma, Unexplained weight loss, Neurological deficits (cauda equina), Age (>50 or <20), Fever/chills, Intravenous drug use, Steroid use, History of cancer.

Exam trap: Never treat unremitting night back pain in an elderly patient with simple physiotherapy without obtaining plain radiographs and inflammatory markers.

[Review note] Option C reads 'Stiffness in the morning for < 30 mm' (the unit should be minutes); source wording preserved.

questions.question: A 13-year-old female gymnast presents with low back pain that is sharply aggravated by repetitive hyperextension of the lumbar spine (such as back walkovers and back handsprings). Physical examination demonstrates focal pain during the single-leg hyperextension (Stork) test. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Repetitive hyperextension and rotation of the lumbar spine in adolescent athletes (gymnasts, divers, figure skaters, football linemen) subjects the pars interarticularis of L5 (and L4) to immense fatigue loading, resulting in a stress fracture of the pars interarticularis known as SPONDYLOLYSIS. Pain is characteristically reproduced by extension and the single-leg hyperextension (Stork) test. (Note: The examination question uses the typo 'Spondylosis' for spondylolysis).

High-yield: Spondylolysis = Stress fracture of the pars interarticularis (most common at L5, 85-90%). Best initial plain film: 45° oblique lumbar radiographs ('collar on the Scottie dog'). Gold standard imaging for active bone stress: SPECT scan or thin-cut bone-window CT / MRI.

Exam trap: Stork Test: Standing on one leg while hyperextending the spine provokes ipsilateral pars pain.

[Review note] Option A uses 'Spondylosis' for spondylolysis; the source acknowledges the typo. Wording preserved.

questions.question: Which of the following is considered an absolute 'Red Flag' in a patient presenting with low back pain?

options.A: hx of cancer (History of prior malignancy)

questions.explanation:
A prior personal history of malignancy (particularly breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid, or melanoma) is the single most predictive clinical red flag for spinal metastasis, carrying a positive likelihood ratio >15. Any patient with a cancer history who develops new back pain requires urgent spinal imaging (MRI with contrast).

High-yield: Primary cancers metastasizing to bone: 'PB-KTL' (Prostate, Breast, Kidney, Thyroid, Lung). Spine is the most common site of skeletal metastases.

Exam trap: Normal plain radiographs do NOT exclude metastatic disease; up to 50% of trabecular bone must be destroyed before a lytic lesion is visible on plain X-ray.

questions.question: Which of the following interventions has been proven to be clinically effective and evidence-based in the management of acute uncomplicated mechanical low back pain?

options.C: Back education program (and maintaining active physical activity)

questions.explanation:
Clinical practice guidelines (American College of Physicians / NICE) strongly recommend that first-line management for acute uncomplicated mechanical low back pain consists of: (1) Patient education regarding the favorable natural history, (2) Advising patients to STAY ACTIVE and avoid prolonged bed rest, and (3) Structured back school / education programs with core ergonomic training. Pharmacotherapy is limited to NSAIDs or muscle relaxants as short-term adjuncts.

High-yield: The single worst recommendation for acute low back pain is STRICT BED REST. Bed rest >48 hours leads to muscle deconditioning, joint stiffness, and chronic disability.

Exam trap: Always advise patients to continue routine activities of daily living within pain tolerance; active movement accelerates recovery.

questions.question: A 30-year-old male presents to the ER with acute low back pain that began yesterday after lifting heavy furniture. History and comprehensive physical examination reveal localized lumbar paraspinal tenderness, normal neurological exam (reflexes, sensation, and motor power 5/5), negative straight leg raise, and absence of red flags. What is the best next step?

options.A: The patient is faking the symptoms and psychological counseling is needed
options.B: Do an X-ray of the lumbar spine
options.D: Prescribe pain relief and follow up (Conservative therapy with NSAIDs and activity)

questions.explanation:
This patient has acute, uncomplicated mechanical lumbar muscular strain (lumbago). In the absence of red flags (fever, weight loss, trauma, cancer history, sphincter dysfunction, progressive neurological deficit), routine imaging (X-rays, MRI) is NOT indicated during the first 4 to 6 weeks. The proper management is conservative: short-term analgesia (NSAIDs, paracetamol), encouragement of normal activity, and outpatient follow-up in 2-4 weeks.

High-yield: American College of Radiology (ACR) Appropriateness Criteria: Acute low back pain without red flags requires NO IMAGING for 6 weeks, as >90% resolve spontaneously.

Exam trap: Ordering routine X-rays or MRI in acute uncomplicated back pain leads to unnecessary interventions on incidental, asymptomatic disc bulges.

optionExplanations.A: Acute muscle strain is a genuine physiological condition.
optionExplanations.B: Routine lumbar plain radiography does not improve clinical outcomes and exposes young gonads to ionizing radiation.
optionExplanations.C: Hospital admission is unnecessary and wasteful for uncomplicated strain.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. This patient has acute, uncomplicated mechanical lumbar muscular strain (lumbago). In the absence of red flags (fever, weight loss, trauma, cancer history, sphincter dysfunction, progressive neurological deficit), routine imaging (X-rays, MRI) is NOT indicated during the first 4 to 6 weeks. The proper management is conservative: short-term analgesia (NSAIDs, paracetamol), encouragement of normal activity, and outpatient follow-up in 2-4 weeks.

questions.question: In adult patients presenting with low back pain, all of the following clinical statements are true EXCEPT:

options.A: Patient profile is helpful in diagnosis and management
options.B: It is a very common presentation in GP clinics
options.C: Infection is more common than mechanical causes
options.D: Ruling out cauda equina is a must
options.E: Spondylolisthesis is one of the causes of LBP in adults

questions.explanation:
Mechanical etiologies (musculoligamentous strain, degenerative disc disease, facet arthropathy, herniated nucleus pulposus) account for over 97% of all low back pain cases. Spinal infections (vertebral osteomyelitis, discitis, epidural abscess) account for LESS THAN 0.01% of presentations in primary care. Stating that infection is more common than mechanical causes is completely false.

High-yield: Etiological Breakdown of Low Back Pain: Mechanical (97%) >> Non-mechanical spinal conditions (neoplasia, infection, inflammatory spondyloarthritis, ~1-2%) >> Visceral referred pain (renal colic, AAA, pancreatitis, ~1%).

Exam trap: Even though infection is rare, never overlook it in high-risk patients (IV drug users, diabetics, hemodialysis patients).

optionExplanations.A: Occupational demands, ergonomics, age, and psychosocial factors ('yellow flags') heavily dictate prognosis.
optionExplanations.B: Low back pain is the second most common symptomatic reason for primary care visits worldwide.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Mechanical etiologies (musculoligamentous strain, degenerative disc disease, facet arthropathy, herniated nucleus pulposus) account for over 97% of all low back pain cases. Spinal infections (vertebral osteomyelitis, discitis, epidural abscess) account for LESS THAN 0.01% of presentations in primary care. Stating that infection is more common than mechanical causes is completely false.

optionExplanations.E: Degenerative or isthmic spondylolisthesis is a frequent structural cause of adult back pain and neurogenic claudication.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that mechanical causes vastly outnumber infectious etiologies in low back pain.

questions.question: A 23-year-old medical student reports a 3-day history of acute, severe atraumatic low back pain that is sharply exacerbated when rotating or flexing his trunk after prolonged studying. Neurological examination is completely unremarkable. What is the most probable cause?

options.D: Muscular pain (Paraspinal muscle spasm / lumbosacral strain)

questions.explanation:
In a healthy, young, afebrile individual presenting with acute atraumatic back pain provoked by postural trunk movements with a completely normal neurological examination, acute lumbosacral muscular strain (paraspinal muscle spasm) is by far the most probable diagnosis (>90% of cases).

High-yield: Postural strain in desk workers results from poor ergonomics and static contraction of the erector spinae and quadratus lumborum muscles.

Exam trap: Do not order an MRI for muscular back strain; clinical diagnosis and reassurance are all that is required.

optionExplanations.A: Herniated disc characteristically presents with dermatomal shooting radicular pain (sciatica), positive straight leg raise, and dermatomal paresthesias.
optionExplanations.B: Discitis presents with systemic fever, elevated ESR/CRP, and severe unremitting night pain.
optionExplanations.C: Multiple myeloma is a disease of older adults (>60 years) presenting with anemia, hypercalcemia, and lytic bone lesions.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. In a healthy, young, afebrile individual presenting with acute atraumatic back pain provoked by postural trunk movements with a completely normal neurological examination, acute lumbosacral muscular strain (paraspinal muscle spasm) is by far the most probable diagnosis (>90% of cases).
optionExplanations.E: Cauda equina presents with urinary retention, saddle anesthesia, and bilateral motor deficits.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify paraspinal muscular strain as the primary etiology of acute atraumatic low back pain in young adults.

questions.question: A 65-year-old lady complains of mild low back pain of 1 week duration. She has a medical history of HTN, DM, and left breast cancer treated surgically 2 years ago. Which of the following serious underlying conditions MUST be definitively ruled out first?
questions.explanation:
In any patient with a verified history of breast adenocarcinoma, new-onset axial skeletal pain is SKELETAL METASTASIS until proven otherwise. Breast carcinoma has high osteotropism; tumor cells disseminate hematogenously via Batson's paravertebral venous plexus to the vertebral bodies. Immediate evaluation with contrast-enhanced spinal MRI is essential to identify epidural compression before irreversible spinal cord damage occurs.

High-yield: Batson's Plexus: Valveless epidural venous system communicating between pelvic/breast veins and the vertebral venous plexus, facilitating retrograde hematogenous tumor dissemination to the spine.

Exam trap: If spinal cord compression (hyperreflexia, upgoing toes, sensory level, weakness) is suspected in a cancer patient, administer high-dose IV dexamethasone IMMEDIATELY prior to obtaining the urgent MRI.

Breast carcinoma has high osteotropism; tumor cells disseminate hematogenously via Batson's paravertebral venous plexus to the vertebral bodies. Immediate evaluation with contrast-enhanced spinal MRI is essential to identify epidural compression before irreversible spinal cord damage occurs.
optionExplanations.B: While common, benign diagnoses cannot be presumed when a fatal oncologic process is in the differential.
optionExplanations.C: While common, benign diagnoses cannot be presumed when a fatal oncologic process is in the differential.

questions.question: The forward translation or slippage of a superior vertebral body over the underlying inferior vertebra, resulting from a bilateral fracture/defect of the pars interarticularis, is formally known as:
questions.explanation:
Spondylolisthesis is the forward translation (slippage) of one vertebral body over another. When caused by a defect (stress fracture or nonunion) of the pars interarticularis (spondylolysis), it is termed ISTHMIC SPONDYLOLISTHESIS (most common at L5-S1). By contrast, DEGENERATIVE spondylolisthesis occurs from facet arthropathy and disc degeneration without a pars defect (most common at L4-L5).

High-yield: Meyerding Classification of Spondylolisthesis (% forward translation): Grade I = <25%; Grade II = 25-50%; Grade III = 50-75%; Grade IV = 75-100%; Grade V = >100% (Spondyloptosis).

Exam trap: Isthmic spondylolisthesis affects L5-S1 in adolescents/young adults; Degenerative spondylolisthesis affects L4-L5 in elderly women.

optionExplanations.B: Spondylosis is a general term for age-related spinal osteoarthritis/degenerative disc disease.

When caused by a defect (stress fracture or nonunion) of the pars interarticularis (spondylolysis), it is termed ISTHMIC SPONDYLOLISTHESIS (most common at L5-S1). By contrast, DEGENERATIVE spondylolisthesis occurs from facet arthropathy and disc degeneration without a pars defect (most common at L4-L5).

questions.question: All of the following are alarming cardinal early clinical presentations of acute Cauda Equina Syndrome (CES) EXCEPT:

options.A: Back pain radiated to both lower limbs
options.B: Bladder and bowel sphincter dysfunction symptoms

questions.explanation:
The acute hallmark cardinal presentation of cauda equina syndrome involves: (1) Severe bilateral sciatica/sciatica, (2) Saddle anesthesia (loss of sensation in the perineum, S3-S5 dermatomes), (3) Bladder and bowel sphincter dysfunction (urinary retention, overflow incontinence, loss of rectal tone), and (4) Bilateral motor weakness in lower extremity muscle groups. While autonomic sexual dysfunction develops as a secondary neurogenic deficit, it is rarely the acute presenting alarm symptom in the emergency triage setting.

High-yield: CES-Incomplete (CESI) vs. CES-Retention (CESR): CESI = Altered urinary sensation, loss of desire to void, straining (reversible if decompressed); CESR = Established painless overflow retention/incontinence (poor recovery even after decompression).

Exam trap: Always perform a digital rectal examination (DRE) to test anal sphincter tone and perianal pinprick sensation in any patient with bilateral sciatica.

[Review note] Source note admits sexual dysfunction is a recognized CES manifestation; key E rests on 'not an acute presenting complaint'. Source key retained.

optionExplanations.B: The core diagnostic tetrad of acute cauda equina syndrome.
optionExplanations.C: The core diagnostic tetrad of acute cauda equina syndrome.
optionExplanations.D: The core diagnostic tetrad of acute cauda equina syndrome.

questions.question: An oblique lumbar spine radiograph demonstrates the classic 'Scottie dog' sign. A radiolucent fracture line crosses the neck of the dog (indicated by the arrows), representing a defect in the pars interarticularis (spondylolysis). Regarding this imaging evaluation, which of the following statements is CORRECT?

options.A: This view is neither AP nor lateral (It is an oblique radiograph)
options.B: This is seen frequently in spina bifida occulta
options.C: Hip osteoarthritis is common with this disease
options.E: Arrows point toward a defect in the facet joint

questions.explanation:
The 'Scottie dog' appearance of the lumbar posterior elements is visualized ONLY on a 45-DEGREE OBLIQUE RADIOGRAPH of the lumbar spine (neither standard AP nor true lateral). The anatomical parts of the Scottie dog correspond to: Superior articular process = Ear; Transverse process = Snout; Pedicle = Eye; Pars interarticularis = Neck; Inferior articular process = Front leg; Lamina = Body. A fracture/defect of the pars interarticularis (spondylolysis) appears as a radiolucent line across the neck ('collar on the Scottie dog').

High-yield: Scottie Dog Anatomy on 45° Oblique View: Nose = Transverse process; Eye = Pedicle; Ear = Superior articular facet; Neck = Pars interarticularis; Front leg = Inferior articular facet. A 'broken neck' (collar) = Spondylolysis.

Exam trap: Pars defects at L5 can be hidden on plain lateral films by the iliac crests; oblique views or sagittal CT reconstructions are required.

Image description (from source; the image itself is not included): 45-degree oblique lumbar spine radiograph showing the posterior elements forming the Scottie dog appearance, with a lucent fracture line across the pars interarticularis ('collar on the dog').

The anatomical parts of the Scottie dog correspond to: Superior articular process = Ear; Transverse process = Snout; Pedicle = Eye; Pars interarticularis = Neck; Inferior articular process = Front leg; Lamina = Body. A fracture/defect of the pars interarticularis (spondylolysis) appears as a radiolucent line across the neck ('collar on the Scottie dog').
